block.title: 🧵 Three Names to Keep in Your Pocket
block.cue: Leaving BSÍ — no window required.
block.hook: Before we point at a single thing, pocket three names: **a painter whose altarpiece got sent back, a brewer who named his beer after a Viking, and a farm boy who won the Nobel Prize.** Their stories are about to keep crashing into each other.
block.point: One valley — **Mosfellsdalur, my literature valley** — ties a Viking's buried silver, a refused painting and a Nobel medal into one stretch of this road.
block.mic: Keep the three names in your pocket. Before the day is out, you will know why the painting, the beer and the book all end up in the same house.
block.weather: Weather pivot: "No window needed for this one, which on a morning like this is just as well."
bullets: **Kjarval** — the painter. His story opens the tour two minutes from now. **He painted more than one altarpiece, and more than one of them got sent back** — and one of the rejects ends up on a wall in a house we pass today. Which one, and what the objection actually was, is a far better story than the one you will find online.

**Tómas** — the brewer. He named his brewery after **Egill Skallagrímsson**, a Viking warrior-poet who could drink a hall dry — and who, as an old man, **buried a fortune in silver** in a valley on today's route.

**Halldór** — the novelist. He grew up in **that same valley**, won Iceland's **only Nobel Prize in Literature** — and **bought the altarpiece nobody else would take** and gave it a wall in his own house. It hangs there still.
say: the painter; his story opens the tour
the brewer who named his beer after a Viking
the farm boy who won the Nobel
the Viking warrior-poet connecting the brewery to the valley
the literature valley where all three threads tie off

block.title: 🧍 Jóhannes Sveinsson Kjarval
block.sub: The Man Who Painted the Ground
block.cue: Look left at 9 o'clock — Klambratún Park.
block.hook: A cod fisherman whose crewmates had a whip-round to send him to art school — and who ended up with **5,405 of his works** in the city's collection and a museum on the hill with his name on it.
block.point: He turned Icelandic painting face-down into the moss, and the city ended up holding five and a half thousand of him.
block.mic: Most countries put a general on the hill. Reykjavík put the man who painted the ground.
block.weather: Weather pivot: "He painted this light, not the postcard light. Grey and wet is the Kjarval palette."
bullets: **Jóhannes Sveinsson Kjarval (1885–1972)** is one of the **central pioneers of modern Icelandic painting** — that is how the museums put it, and it is the honest framing. "Iceland's greatest painter" is an opinion, however widely held.

He came to it the hard way, off a fishing boat, and trained in **Copenhagen**. What he did with it was the un-obvious thing: he **got down on the ground**. Icelandic landscape painting had been all mountains and distance; Kjarval knelt over the **moss, the lava and the cracks** and painted the three feet in front of his face.

In among the rock he painted **faces and figures** — that is real, and it is where the elf stories come from. But be careful with it on the mic: the **fantasy forms appear in parts of his work**, not in every canvas, and **not every odd-shaped rock he painted is a documented hidden person.** The lava is the subject. The faces are the seasoning.

**Kjarvalsstaðir**, on **Klambratún**, opened in **1973** — the formal opening was **24 March** — and was designed by **Hannes Kr. Davíðsson**. It is **one of the three buildings of Reykjavík Art Museum**, alongside **Hafnarhús** and **Ásmundarsafn**. It carries special responsibility for his work, but it is a general exhibition space too, not a one-man shrine.

The numbers behind that responsibility are startling. The city's own 2019 operating report lists its registered Kjarval holdings as **5,405 works** — **195 paintings, 5,167 drawings and 43 other pieces** — out of **17,495** works in the whole museum collection. **He is very nearly a third of it.**

And the honours story is better than the version you usually hear. He did **not** simply refuse the **Order of the Falcon** out of modesty. An honour proposed in **1965** was **initially declined**, and what followed was a negotiated arrangement, with the insignia ending up associated with the **National Gallery**. A man who said no, then let them find a way round him.
say: the museum on Klambratún named for him
the architect who designed it, opened 1973
Reykjavík Art Museum, its three houses
the Order of the Falcon he first turned down

block.title: 🏢 Ölgerðin Egill Skallagrímsson
block.cue: Look right at 3 o'clock — Egils Brewery.
block.hook: A brewery founded in **1913** — and **two years later Iceland banned the lot.** It is still here. It outlasted the ban by seventy-four years and then sold the country its Christmas drink.
block.point: Founded two years before the ban, and it sold the country malt, orange fizz and 2.25% beer until the law came to its senses.
block.mic: Iceland let you drink brandy before it let you drink lager. This lot waited seventy-four years and kept the lights on with fizzy orange.
block.weather: Weather pivot: "Malt and Appelsín is a cold-weather drink anyway. Today is basically a Christmas advert."
bullets: **Tómas Tómasson** founded **Ölgerðin Egill Skallagrímsson** in **1913**, and the company's own history dates the first production and delivery to **17 April**. A newspaper from **March 1914** already names him as owner and notes he had worked at the **Sanitas** soft-drink factory — so he learned fizz before he learned beer.

It is named after the saga poet and warrior **Egill Skallagrímsson**. The company links him to ale; **why Tómas actually picked him is not recorded anywhere I can stand behind**, so anyone who tells you it was because Egill was a famous drinker is guessing.

**Prohibition did not arrive in one go.** The law was passed on **30 July 1909**; the **import ban** bit on **1 January 1912**; the **general sales ban** on **1 January 1915**. **Wine came back in 1922**, **spirits in January 1935** after a referendum — and **beer stayed illegal until 1 March 1989.** Seventy-four years. A country that allowed you brandy but not lager.

Here is the part everyone gets wrong: **"pilsner" was never alcohol-free.** Icelandic law set the line at **2.25% ABV** — at or below that, a drink was legally not *áfengi* at all. So the shelves held real, weak beer the whole time. Ölgerðin sold **malt drinks, soft drinks and 2.25% beer** for three generations.

And there was one loophole with a uniform on. From **1940** Ölgerðin brewed **Polar Ale for the occupying forces**, whose bases sat outside the domestic rules. **Full-strength beer was being made in Reykjavík — Icelanders just were not allowed to buy it.**
**1 March 1989**, beer came back, and Icelanders called it **Bjórdagur** — Beer Day. Not an official holiday. Just a nation marking the end of the daftest rule it ever wrote.

The other legacy is in every fridge at Christmas: **Egils Malt mixed with Appelsín**, the orange fizz. The argument about **which one you pour first** is genuinely national, and there is **no single correct ratio** — anyone insisting on equal parts is stating a preference, not a tradition.

One modern footnote, because it changed six months ago: in **February 2026** shareholders renamed the listed parent company **Bera hf.** — the Nasdaq Iceland ticker went **OLGERD → BERA on 4 March 2026** — and the drinks business now trades as **Ölgerðin Egill Skallagrímsson ehf.** The brewery is still at **Grjótháls**. Same beer, new letterhead.
say: the saga poet and warrior it is named for
light beer, at or under the 2.25% legal line
the orange fizz mixed with Malt at Christmas
the Reykjavík street the brewery still sits on

block.title: 🏞️ Elliðaárdalur
block.sub: The Valley That Runs the City
block.cue: Look right at 2 o'clock — Elliðaárdalur.
block.hook: Most capitals get a grey, sad little river. Reykjavík's hands you **dinner, drinking water, electricity — and an argument about where parliament started.** Show-off.
block.point: One small river feeds the city, waters it, lit it, and holds the argument about where its parliament began. Most capitals would settle for the water.
block.mic: We counted the salmon with a camera, bought the river outright, and got a king to pull the switch. For a stream you could throw a stone across, it has had a career.
block.weather: Weather pivot: "In this you will not see much of the valley — but you are driving over the river that runs the whole city, and that is the point of it."
bullets: Meet the **Elliðaá** — one of very few **capital-city rivers anywhere with a wild Atlantic salmon run.** And I can give you the real count, because they put a **camera counter** in it: in **2009** the whole run was **1,533 fish** — **1,242 through the counter and 291 caught below it** — and the report is explicit that these were **naturally produced salmon, because no smolts had been released the previous year.** In **2003** it was **1,067**. (If you have heard "two and a half thousand salmon", that number is real but it is the wrong animal: **2,500 is a batch of smolts**, not returning adults. I have said it wrong myself.)

The stock has been **monitored continuously since 1988**. It **crashed in 1997**, they moved fish and stocked fry where spawning had failed — and the line that matters is this one: **all stocking has since been stopped, because the run now renews itself.**
The city was so taken with the river it **bought it in 1906**, for hydro power. (Your city buys parks. We bought a river.)

**The tap water your hotel keeps bragging about starts here too.** **Vatnsveita Reykjavíkur was formally founded on 16 June 1909**; water was taken **straight out of the Elliðaár that summer**, and from **Gvendarbrunnar**, the springs by **Elliðavatn**, later the same year. Two different supplies, same valley — and the Gvendarbrunnar water is the one you are drinking.

**The lights: Elliðaárstöð, switched on 27 June 1921** — and not metaphorically. **King Christian X and Queen Alexandrine were inside the station and started the first two machines themselves.** It opened as a **1,500-horsepower plant producing 1,000 kW**, and was expanded over the years to about **3,150 kW by 1933.** I will not tell you it was Iceland's second power station or its biggest, because **neither of those rankings survives checking** — plenty of small plants were already running by 1921.

**Iceland's first was humbler.** In **1904** the Hafnarfjörður carpenter **Jóhannes Reykdal**, with **Halldór Guðmundsson**, wired a **9 kW** generator to his workshop stream and lit **sixteen houses and four street lamps.** Officially the country's first power station. Realistically, a shed with big ideas.

Upstream, on a low spit in **Elliðavatn** called **Þingnes**, sits a cluster of settlement-age ruins the state registers as *hinn forni Kjalarnessþingstaður* — the ancient Kjalarnes assembly place. **Whether it actually is is a genuinely open question and always has been.** Six seasons of excavation never settled it; **Adolf Friðriksson's position is that the archaeology does not establish a þing-site at all.** **Ari fróði** put that assembly on **Kjalarnes**; the ruins are here, **fourteen kilometres away**, and nobody has ever closed the gap. And the old ground now lies **partly underwater** since the river was dammed. Very Icelandic: invent democracy, mislay it, then flood it.

**The heat, too — and this surprises people.** Reykjavík's hot water did not start with a volcano out in the lava. It started **inside the city**: **low-temperature fields at Laugarnes and here in Elliðaárdalur**, plus **Mosfellsbær** out of town. Those wells still work, and neighbourhoods get deliberately swapped between sources **so the reservoir under the city can rest.** Yes — the ground gets a lie-down.
say: the valley that feeds, waters and powers the capital
the river itself, with a counted, self-renewing salmon run
the lake upstream; Gvendarbrunnar beside it gives the city its water
"Guðmundur's springs", the source of Reykjavík's tap water since 1909
the 1921 power station a king and queen switched on in person
the spit with the ruins the state calls the old Kjalarnes assembly place; the identification is unproven
the Hafnarfjörður carpenter whose 9 kW shed came first, in 1904

block.title: ⛰️ Mount Esja
block.cue: Look left and ahead — the long striped wall of Esja.
block.hook: That is not a mountain. It is **at least two dead volcanoes wearing one name** — and the honest position is that **nobody can tell you exactly how old it is or exactly how tall the top is.**
block.point: Two dead volcanoes, a stack of ice ages, and not one agreed number on the whole thing — and the city still checks it every single morning.
block.mic: This is the most looked-at mountain in Iceland and we cannot tell you for certain how old it is or how tall it is. Dark bands warm, pale bands frozen. That part we are sure about.
block.weather: Weather pivot: "If Esja has gone, you are getting the honest version. Locals judge the whole day by how much of it they can see."
bullets: **It is not one mountain, and it is certainly not one volcano.** The rock records **more than one extinct central volcano**: an older **Kjalarnes** centre in the west — which some publications call **Viðeyjareldstöðin**, and whether those are one volcano or two is still argued over — and the younger **Stardalur** central volcano in the east, with its own caldera. Volcanism migrated **eastward** across the whole pile. "Esja" is the name of the eroded mountain mass you are looking at. It is not the name of a volcano.

**The stripes are climate, and you can read them from your seat.** **Dark basalt** flowed in warm, ice-free spells and cooled in peace. **Pale móberg** is lava that picked a fight with a glacier and lost — erupted under ice, shattered, welded into rubble. **Dark means warm. Pale means frozen.** That is the whole code, and it is the one part of this mountain nobody disputes.

**How many ice ages are stacked in there? Here is the honest answer.** The peer-reviewed survey — **Leó Kristjánsson, Ingvar Birgir Friðleifsson and Norman D. Watkins** — logged a **2,100-metre composite section across Akrafjall, Eyrarfjall and Esja** and read **at least 11, possibly 16 glaciations** in it, plus **at least 13** across western and south-west Iceland between **3.1 and 1.8 million years ago**. But **that count is for the composite, not for Esja on its own** — several of the lower horizons sit in Akrafjall and Eyrarfjall before the section even reaches this mountain. So you are looking at a stack of ice ages. The number everybody quotes belongs to a bigger profile than the thing out the window.

**How old? Also genuinely disputed.** That composite section is dated **4.2 to 1.8 million years**. Two University of Iceland theses put Esja's oldest rock at **2.8 million years** and the youngest Stardalur rhyolite at **1.8** — but both trace back through the same 1985 account, so that is **one source wearing two hats**. And the actual **potassium–argon measurements** on the upper rhyolite come out at **1.89 ± 0.08**, **1.78 ± 0.04** and **1.85 ± 0.18 million years.** "Exactly 1.8" is a rounded interpretation, not a reading off a machine.

**The heights are not settled either**, which for the most-looked-at object in Reykjavík is quietly hilarious. **Hábunga** is the name usually given to the true summit at **914 m** — not confirmed against any official survey record I would stand behind. **Þverfellshorn**, the one everybody actually climbs, is usually quoted at **780 m**; the nearest real published measurement is a **weather station at 783 m** *near* Þverfell, which is a different object on a different spot. And the boulder called **Steinn** is a genuinely documented route landmark — a **kennileiti** — but it has **no registered elevation anywhere.** Touch the rock and you have climbed Esja. Nobody checks. Nobody could.
**Which is exactly how the city uses it anyway.** Reykjavíkers do not open the weather app. They look out of the window and see whether Esja is still there.
say: the striped mass on the skyline; an eroded pile, not a single volcano
the older, western extinct central volcano inside it
the other name some publications give that same older centre
the younger central volcano in the east, with its own caldera
the name usually given to the true summit, quoted at 914 m
the peak everyone actually hikes, quoted at 780 m
"the Stone", the boulder where hikers turn round; a documented landmark with no registered height
the pale rock: lava that erupted under ice and shattered
"a landmark"; what the sources actually call Steinn

block.title: ⚖️ Kjalarnesþing
block.cue: Look left at 9 o'clock — across Kollafjörður to Kjalarnes, under the foot of Esja, four kilometres off. We turn east before it.
block.hook: Iceland's world-famous parliament at Þingvellir? Not even the first. There was a **Kjalarnesþing** before it, set up by the founder's son. Nepotism: also a Viking value.
block.point: Iceland's first parliament is a place we can name and cannot find. The text says Kjalarnes, the ruins are fourteen kilometres away, and a thousand years on nobody has closed the gap.
block.mic: Kjalarnes did the homework. Þingvellir took the credit, the fame, and the tourists.
block.weather: Weather pivot: "Esja above it decides the visibility — if the mountain has gone, so has the headland. Though honestly there is nothing to see on the clearest day either. It is a field. The story is the thing, not the view."
bullets: **Ari fróði** wrote the only near-contemporary line about it, around **1122–33**, and it is worth having in full: *"Alþingi var sett at ráði Úlfljóts ok allra landsmanna þar es nú es, **en áðr var þing á Kjalarnesi**, þat es **Þorsteinn Ingólfssonr** landnámsmanns … hafði þar ok höfðingjar þeir es at því hurfu."* Before the Alþingi, a þing on Kjalarnes, held by the first settler's son and the chieftains who joined him.

Notice what Ari does **not** say. He gives no meeting place, describes no structures, does not call it a vorþing, and never says it was Iceland's first. **Jakob Benediktsson** flagged the open question: was it a district assembly, or an embryo of the national one? Even "the parliament before the parliament" is an interpretation.

**And nothing has ever been found on Kjalarnes.** The candidate everyone points at is **Leiðvöllur**, a gravel spit out past **Mógilsá** on the north side of Kollafjörður. **Sigurður Vigfússon** searched it properly — the spit, the slope above it, both sides of the channel — and published in the **1880–81 Árbók**. He found **one very indistinct small ruin**. His answer was to suppose the sea had eaten the site, which is a hypothesis, not a find.

The ruins are **13.8 km south**, at **Þingnes** on **Elliðavatn** — and that is where **Jónas Hallgrímsson** actually dug, on **21 June 1841**, with four hired labourers. He counted **about twenty ruins** plus a stone circle, opened the biggest, and reasoned that a þing-site this size in this district could hardly be anything but the Kjalarnesþing. Morphology, density and the name **Þingnes**. No inscription, no dated find.

The National Museum went back for **six seasons, 1981 to 1986**, under **Guðmundur Ólafsson**. The 1984 instrument survey recorded **16–17 surface ruins and at least 18 structures** — and they are **not all booths**: one looks like a permanently occupied house, one held **slag** and reads as a smithy, and some unexcavated ones may be later sheep houses or barns.

The famous **"judgement ring"** is two circles, not one: an outer ring built **purely of stone**, about **18–20 m overall and 14–15 m inside**, with a smaller **turf** circle nested in it and paving from a different phase inside that. **No entrance was ever found.** Guðmundur allowed it might be a **lögrétta** — and also weighed a livestock pen, which the central position and missing doorway argue against. The archaeology calls them *circular structures* and leaves the function open. **"Dómhringur" is an antiquarian label, not a result.**

**There is no radiocarbon date from Þingnes at all** — the 2004 report says plainly that its charcoal was never submitted. What the ground gives is tephra: the **Landnám ash (c. 871)** sits *inside the turf* of several walls, so those walls were cut and built after it. At one structure the activity layer lay **3.5 cm** above that ash, and at an assumed **1 mm a year** that works out at the **early 900s** — the report calls that an estimate, and it is. Activity runs from about **900 into the 1200s**.

So: **plausible, unproven, and the experts have never agreed.** **Kålund** accepted it looked like a þing-site but said it was unresolved whether Kjalarnesþing ever met there. **Brynjúlfur Jónsson** thought it might be a single chieftaincy's assembly instead. **Guðmundur Ólafsson** called Kjalarnesþing the obvious candidate and stated outright that it could not be asserted as certain. **Adolf Friðriksson** went further: the archaeology does not independently establish a þing-site at all.

The state, meanwhile, wrote it down as fact and never took it back. The register reads *"Mannvirkjaleifar á **hinum forna Kjalarnessþingstað** í Þingnesi"* — **signed 25 October 1930, registered 16 November 1938** (so if the sign at the lake says 1938, it is not contradicting you — that is the second date). **Inherited legal wording, not archaeological proof.**

**Footnote from the same peninsula, and it is a good one.** Landnámabók has **Örlygur Hrappsson** building a church at **Esjuberg** in the settlement period — by tradition Iceland's earliest. In **1981** the National Museum opened the mound locals call **Kirkjurúst Örlygs**, the ruin of Örlygur's church. It turned out to be an outbuilding from the **16th or 17th century**. A debris slide off the gully above has since buried the ground around it, so Guðmundur concluded further digging there would be pointless. The church may well be under the landslide. It has simply never been found.

The laws, at least, are solid. The chieftains sent one man — **Úlfljótr** — to **Norway for three winters** to learn the **Gulating law** and adapt it. Nothing was written down, so he **carried the whole code home in his head**, and it came back with one radical edit the Norwegians never made: a parliament with **no king**. Stole the software, deleted the boss.

And the line everyone hangs on him — **"með lögum skal land byggja"** — **he almost certainly never said.** Its first appearance in Icelandic writing is **Njáls saga, chapter 70**; it enters Icelandic *law* only with **Járnsíða**, the Norwegian king's code of **1271–74**, and it is **not in Grágás** at all. The phrasing comes from Norway's **Frostaþingslög**. Roughly **three and a half centuries** too young to be his.
say: the assembly Ari places on Kjalarnes, before the Alþingi
the first settler's son, who held it
"the Wise", who wrote the one near-contemporary sentence about it
the gravel spit past Mógilsá searched, and found empty, in 1880
the spit on Elliðavatn where the ruins actually are
the farm whose "church of Örlygur" turned out to be a 16th-century shed
sent to Norway for three winters to bring the first law code home in his head
the Norwegian law he studied and adapted
the Norwegian code of 1271–74 that brought the famous phrase into Icelandic law

block.title: 🎵 Mosfellsbær
block.sub: A Town That Punches Above Its Weight
block.cue: All around — Mosfellsbær.
block.hook: A commuter town of **~13,700** — smaller than a single Reykjavík suburb — that exported **two global music acts** at opposite ends of the volume knob.
block.point: A town this size shouldn't manage one global act. Mosfellsbær made two — whisper-quiet piano and stadium blues, from the same patch of moss.
block.mic: Two acts, one small town, zero chill.
block.weather: Weather pivot: "Low cloud suits this valley. Half the music that came out of it sounds like this weather."
bullets: **Ólafur Arnalds**, born here **1986**: **won the 2014 BAFTA TV Craft Award** for scoring ITV's *Broadchurch*, and picked up **two Grammy nominations** at the 2021 awards besides. For his *Island Songs* project (2016) he wrote **seven tracks in seven weeks at seven spots** around Iceland — one, *"Particles,"* with **Nanna Bryndís** of Of Monsters and Men.
🎵 *Now playing — "Particles," Ólafur Arnalds feat. Nanna Bryndís Hilmarsdóttir*

Loud end of the dial: **Kaleo**, the blues-rock band formed here in **2012**, whose *"Way Down We Go"* hit **No. 1** on the US alternative chart. Their *"Vor í Vaglaskógi"* is a smoky cover of an Icelandic classic about a forest up north.
🎵 *Now playing — "Vor í Vaglaskógi," Kaleo*

There is a second history under the music. After the British landed on **10 May 1940** the Americans took over in **July 1941**, and the US Army's own medical history puts **80% of the entire American force in Iceland** in a coastal strip **centred on Álafoss** — this town. In **April 1942** the **167th Station Hospital** moved into fresh **Nissen huts at Álafoss**, and they plumbed the **hot springs** in to heat the wards. A field hospital, warmed by the ground.

It is still in the soil. Minjastofnun's **2022 survey at Lágafell** records a circular **gun-pit, 3.5 by 3.1 metres**, and an intact **34-metre trench** — both still there. **Lágafell Camp** itself, a depot and vehicle workshop on land requisitioned from **Thor Jensen**, has vanished completely under later housing. The camp went. The hole somebody dug to shoot from did not.

Up the coast at **Hvalfjörður** the Royal Navy ran **HMS Baldur** at **Hvítanes** from 1940 to the end of the war, and the Americans built a fuel depot of **44 oil tanks**. **Convoy PQ17 sailed out of that fjord on 27 June 1942** — **35 merchant ships** bound for **Arkhangelsk**. **Eleven arrived.** And a myth worth killing: **HMS Hood did not sail from Hvalfjörður** on her last voyage — she was on her way *to* it when she was turned west for the Bismarck.
say: the commuter town all around us, about 13,700 people
the composer born here in 1986, the quiet end of the volume knob
the blues-rock band formed here in 2012, the loud end
of Of Monsters and Men; she sings on Particles
the Kaleo track, a cover of an Icelandic classic about a forest up north
the old wool mill here, the centre of the American camps
'Whale fjord', up the coast, the Arctic convoy anchorage
the point in that fjord where the Royal Navy base stood

block.title: 🪶 Mosfellsdalur
block.sub: A Valley of Buried Silver and a Nobel Prize
block.cue: All around — Mosfellsdalur.
block.hook: Two famous residents, a thousand years apart: one **buried a fortune here and killed the witnesses**; the other won the **Nobel Prize**.
block.point: A buried fortune no-one's ever found, and a Nobel written five minutes up the road from it.
block.mic: One man hid his fortune. The other left his on the shelves.
block.weather: Weather pivot: "If the valley has closed in, so much the better. Laxness wrote most of it looking at exactly this."
bullets: **The silver (from Egil's saga):** in old age the warrior-poet **Egill Skallagrímsson** — sitting on two chests of silver gifted by **King Æthelstan of England** (the same Egill the brewery back in town is named after) — slipped off during the Alþingi with the silver, a horse and two slaves. The horse came back. Egill came back. The slaves and the silver didn't — he killed them to keep the spot secret. A thousand years of treasure hunters later: score **zero**. (Saga, not survey — treat it as legend.)
**The dig:** archaeologists have excavated nearby at **Hrísbrú**, where the saga says Egil's bones were later moved to the church his descendants built.

**The Nobel:** born **Halldór Guðjónsson** in **1902**, raised from age three at the farm **Laxnes** just here in the valley — when he needed an author's name, **he took the farm's**. **Nobel Prize for Literature, 1955** — Iceland's only laureate, largely for ***Sjálfstætt fólk*** (*Independent People*).
Two places in this valley, a few hundred metres apart: **Laxnes**, the farm that gave him his name, and **Gljúfrasteinn**, the house he built with the proceeds.

born 1902, grew up in this valley, Iceland's only Nobel laureate

block.title: 🎬 Laxnes Horse Farm
block.cue: Look left on Route 36 — Laxnes, about 400 metres up the side road.
block.hook: That farm started with **six horses and one stranger asking for a ride.** Its horses have since turned up in *Game of Thrones* — and the boy who grew up on this land carried the farm's name all the way to Stockholm.
block.point: One small farm exported a breed to Hollywood **and** a surname to Stockholm.
block.mic: Some of these horses grazing by the road have better screen credits than most working actors. Don't ask for autographs — they only sign with a hoof.
block.weather: Weather pivot: "The horses do not mind, and they will be out in it. They were bred for days like this."
bullets: **Ragnheiður Gíslason** and **Þórarinn "Þóri" Jónasson** moved onto the run-down farm in **1967** and started the riding business in **1968**, after a visitor asked out of nowhere whether they'd take him out on horseback. Six horses, summers only. It grew into **Iceland's oldest continuously running riding-tour company** — **120 horses** and around **15,000 riders a year** by **2018**, **85% of them from abroad**.

Their horses work on screen too. The Mosfellsbær local paper *Mosfellingur* puts it plainly: **"hestar frá Laxnesi birst í nokkrum bíómyndum eins og Game of Thrones"** — horses from Laxnes have appeared in several films, *Game of Thrones* among them. In **1992** Þóri shipped Icelandic horses to the **United States** to show them off near Hollywood and ended up on **CBS and CNN**.

And the name. **Halldór Guðjónsson** was raised on this farm from the age of **three**. When he started publishing he took the farm's name — **Laxness** — and in **1955** that name won Iceland's **only Nobel Prize in Literature**. **Gljúfrasteinn**, the white house he built with the proceeds, is **600 metres along the valley** from this gate.
say: riding tours since 1968, and the boyhood home that gave Halldór his pen-name
the valley it sits in, off Route 36
co-founder, who moved onto the farm in 1967
the boy from this farm; Nobel Prize, 1955

block.title: 🪶 Gljúfrasteinn
block.cue: Look right — the white house by the river Kaldakvísl, just off Route 36.
block.hook: On **17 June 1945** — the young republic's first birthday — a woman sat down and typed the building contract for that white house. **Ten years later there was a Nobel Prize in it.**
block.point: Iceland's only Nobel came home to a quiet valley — to a house that doubles as the country's smallest gallery of rejected art.
block.mic: A Nobel on the shelf, a rejected altarpiece on the wall — Gljúfrasteinn is where Iceland keeps the things the gatekeepers got wrong.
block.weather: Weather pivot: "A white house in grey rain is very Icelandic literature. He would have approved."
bullets: The typist was **Auður Sveinsdóttir**, born at **Eyrarbakki on 30 July 1918**, and she didn't just type it — she ran the build. She married **Halldór Laxness** that **Christmas Eve, 1945**. The architect was **Ágúst Pálsson**; the house was home from **1945** until Halldór died on **8 February 1998**. Auður outlived him by fourteen years, dying **29 October 2012**, aged **94**.

**1955:** Halldór takes Iceland's **only Nobel Prize in Literature** — *"for his vivid epic power which has renewed the great narrative art of Iceland."* Auður marked it the way a textile artist would: she made **Maríuklæðið**, "Mary's Cloth", to commemorate it.

**Kjarval's altarpieces, chapter one:** in **1914** the people of **Borgarfjörður eystri** commissioned him to paint one for their church at **Bakkagerði**, and the women of the district kept him fed while he worked on it. It is still there. And the famous part — that the rock Christ preaches from is **Álfaborg, the elf city**, with **Dyrfjöll** behind — is the reading absolutely everybody gives it, **including me**, but **no church, museum or art-historical source documents Kjarval ever saying so**, and nobody has produced a record of a bishop refusing to bless it. It is a wonderful story. I am telling you it is a story.

**Chapter two, and this one is documented — by the museum that owns it.** Kjarval painted an altarpiece for **Rípurkirkja** in Skagafjörður. In **1925**, **after the church had already been consecrated**, the clergy turned the painting down, and their objection is on record: *"Þetta er söguleg fölsun. Hér sýnir málarinn Krist sem ungling, en Jóhannes skírara sem öldung"* — this is a historical falsification; the painter shows **Christ as a youth and John the Baptist as an old man.** Not blasphemy. **Bad chronology.**

The picture then wandered. It ended up with a farmer called **Ólafur**, and when he died **his widow wrote to Halldór and offered it to him.** He took it. It hangs in the **entrance hall** of this house — so the first thing you see on the way in is a painting a parish sent back.

**And there is a coda.** Kjarval came here later to sign it, and while he had the brush out he wanted to **add a beard to John the Baptist.** Halldór stopped him. **You can still see the faint marks he got in before he was stopped.** The painter, the brewer's Viking and the novelist — the morning's three pocket names — all tie off in this one valley.

The **Icelandic state bought the house and its art in 2002**, a hundred years to the year since Halldór was born, and opened it to the public on **4 September 2004**. His **typewriter is still on the desk**.
say: the poet's house: home from 1945, museum since 2004, typewriter still on the desk

block.title: 🚢 The Norse Expansion (793–1066 CE)
block.cue: Approaching Þingvellir.
bullets: **Social** — competition among ambitious young men (polygyny, inheritance); population outgrew the land.
**Economic** — silver, silk, spices, and a profitable **slave trade**.
**Political** — retaliation against Christian encroachment; warfare brought status and new land.
**🌊 Expansion routes**
**Raids & trade — who, why, what moved**
| **Region** | **Main targets** | **Why they came** | **Took/traded (N→S)** | **Got back (S→N)** |
| England | Monasteries, towns | Wealth, slaves, land | Furs, amber, slaves, timber | Silver, gold, weapons |
| Ireland | Monasteries, towns | Wealth, slaves, trade towns | Furs, amber, slaves, timber | Silver, gold, weapons |
| Scotland | Islands, towns | Land, cattle, slaves | Furs, amber, timber | Silver, weapons |
| France | River towns, Paris | Ransom, loot, settlement | Furs, amber, timber, slaves | Silver, silk, weapons |
| Spain/Portugal | Coastal cities | Slaves, spices, plunder | Furs, amber, timber, slaves | Silver, gold, silk, spices |
| Low Countries | Coastal towns | Trade control, markets | Furs, amber, timber, slaves | Silver, gold, luxury goods |
| Baltic | Trading centres | Furs, amber, slaves | Furs, amber, timber, slaves | Silver, silk, spices |
| Eastern Europe | River trade towns | River-route control, silver | Furs, amber, slaves, timber | Silver (Arab coins), silk, spices |
| North Atlantic | Islands, new land | Farmland, resources | Furs, amber, timber, walrus ivory | Silver, weapons, exotic goods |
| Morocco | Nekor, 858–859 (al-Bakrī) | Gold, silver, fame | Slaves, furs, amber, timber | Gold, silver, spices, textiles |
**🗺️ Patterns**

**North → South:** furs, amber, slaves, timber, walrus ivory — raided and traded out of monasteries, river towns and coastal cities from **Ireland to Morocco** (yes, Morocco — the **Nekor raid, 858–859**).
**South → North:** **silver** (Islamic dirhams), **silk**, spices, weapons, luxury goods.
**Reach:** sea + river networks linking the Arctic to the Mediterranean — **6,000+ miles**, Baghdad to Ireland.
**🌏 What they achieved**
Trade network: Volga → the Islamic world, Dnieper → Byzantium, Atlantic → western Europe and North America.
Arabic silver coins turning up in Scandinavian hoards; deep slave networks; whole new markets stitched together.

**Vínland — the one hard proof, and it is now dated to the year.** The Norse site at **L'Anse aux Meadows**, Newfoundland — **found by Helge and Anne Stine Ingstad in 1960**, the Norse remains confirmed by excavation **from 1962**, **UNESCO-listed 1978** — is the **only confirmed Norse archaeological site in North America.** In **2021** a *Nature* study found the **993 cosmic-ray radiocarbon spike** in three wood samples and counted the rings out to the bark: **the trees were felled in 1021.** That is **471 years before Columbus reached the Caribbean in 1492** — and be precise about what it dates: **1021 is when they cut wood there**, not when they arrived or how long they stayed.

Legacy: English law and language, the sagas, **the Alþingi — founded around 930 and one of the world's oldest parliamentary institutions** (say it that way: the year is a reconstruction, and it was **abolished in 1800 and restored in 1845**) — plus the birth of **Normandy** and **Kievan Rus'**.
**⏳ How it ended (1066)**

**Battle of Stamford Bridge, 1066** — Harald Hardrada's defeat is the traditional close of the Viking Age. That is the British frame: **the British Museum and Denmark's National Museum both use about 800 to 1050**, and archaeologists commonly use **750 to 1050**. Same centuries, different bookends.
Why: political consolidation, Christianization, stronger defences, climate cooling, a shift to legal trade.
**🗝️ Key dates**

block.title: 🏘️ Landnám
block.sub: Sixty Years to Build a Country
block.cue: Crossing the Settlement Era.
block.hook: By tradition, in **874 CE** Iceland was all but empty. By **930**, it was full. Settled, mapped and **booted up with a national parliament** — in a single human lifetime.
block.point: Most countries are built over centuries by armies. Iceland was built in **two generations**, by farmers with notebooks.
block.mic: Founding-fathers? We've got 400. We named them all. They're still in the book.
block.weather: Weather pivot: "No view required. This is the chapter you listen to rather than look at."
bullets: The **Landnám** ("Land-Taking") is the **~60-year window** when 9,000-plus Norse, Celtic and other settlers grabbed every habitable bay and valley on the island. (**874 is the traditional date**; Ari the Wise points nearer **870**, and a nationwide ash layer — the **871 ± 2 tephra** — timestamps the whole business to the second.)
The textbook source is **Landnámabók** (*The Book of Settlements*) — **400 settlers** named, their farms, feuds and home-towns mapped in detail no other Viking-age country can match.
The trick: Iceland had **no locals to fight** — just a handful of Irish monks (the **Papar**) who legged it the moment longships appeared.
By **930** the population (and the feuds) were big enough that the chieftains met at **Þingvellir** to launch the **Alþingi**, the world's oldest parliament still in use.
say: the Land-Taking, the sixty years when settlers filled the island
The Book of Settlements, which names 400 of them
the Irish monks who legged it when the longships appeared
the national parliament launched at Þingvellir in 930

block.title: 🌍 Almannagjá
block.cue: We are walking down inside the crack. The wall on your left is the edge of North America.
block.hook: You are in the **gap between two continents** — and no, they do not meet here. They are tearing **apart**, at the speed your fingernails grow, and this valley is the hole they have left behind.
block.point: Most plate boundaries sit invisible under two kilometres of ocean. Here you can **walk into the one the planet is tearing open.**
block.mic: Hand on the wall to your left: North America. It is going that way. You are going that way. Slowly, and there is no hurry — it is about as fast as your fingernails grow.
block.weather: Weather pivot: "Rain in the rift is normal. The wall does not care, and neither did the men who argued under it."
bullets: Forget the postcard version where you "touch two continents at once." **Þingvellir** sits on the **Mid-Atlantic Ridge**, and what you are standing in is a **seven-kilometre-wide graben** — a strip of valley floor **sinking between two fault walls** as the plates pull apart about **2 cm a year**. The plates never touch here. The valley **is** the gap.

The cracks have names. **Almannagjá**, the big one you are walking through, is the **torn edge on the North American side**; its twin **Heiðargjá** marks the far side of the rift. The floor between them belongs to **neither continent** — it is the seam, still ripping.
The plain is **Þingvallahraun**, a **9,000-year-old** shield lava that spread down from **Skjaldbreiður**. Since then the floor has sunk **over 40 m** and the rift has pulled open by about **70 m**.

It does not creep smoothly — it locks, strains, then lets go. The last big pulse came in **spring 1789**, dropping the valley floor about **2.5 m in roughly ten days** and flooding the paths around the assembly ground.
Since **930** the assembly ground itself has dropped some **3–4 m.** The parliament you are about to stand in met noticeably higher up than the ground you are on.

🎬 **On screen:** this gorge is the pass to the **Bloody Gate** in *Game of Thrones* — the gate was added digitally above the Öxarárfoss trail — and the park doubled as an otherworldly realm in ***Thor: The Dark World*** (2013).
say: the big crack you walk through; its west wall is the edge of the North American plate
the fault marking the far side of the rift
the 9,000-year-old lava plain the valley floor is made of
the shield volcano that poured it out

block.title: ⚖️ Lögberg & the Alþingi
block.cue: At the Law Rock — the wall behind you is the reason this spot was chosen.
block.hook: The **world's oldest parliament still in use**. Set up in **930 CE** in a literal **crack in the earth** — because the acoustics were better than anyone's farmhouse.
block.point: No royal palace. No marble columns. Just a rock, a cliff wall, and the world's first national parliament held outdoors.
block.mic: Britain calls itself the home of parliament. Iceland was running one **300 years before the Magna Carta** — in a hole in the ground.
block.weather: Weather pivot: "They met here for two weeks every summer in whatever the sky was doing. So can we."
bullets: In **930 CE**, Iceland's chieftains gathered here and founded the **Alþingi** — the national assembly. They picked the spot because the **Lögberg** ("Law Rock") cliff wall **carried the spoken law** across the valley.
For two weeks every summer the country **shut down** and came here: laws made, marriages arranged, murderers tried, beer drunk.

The **Lögsögumaður** (Law-Speaker), elected for a **three-year term**, had to recite **a third of the entire legal code from memory each year** — three years to deliver the lot. Drop one clause and you could change a verdict.
And there was **no king** — roughly **36 goðar** (chieftain-priests) ran the whole thing by consensus. One law, one people, zero crowns.

They chose this ground carefully: reachable from north, south and west inside about **seventeen days' travel**, a natural stage of cliffs and level floor, and **common land confiscated after its owner was outlawed for murder.** Practical, dramatic and pointedly neutral.

It met here every summer until **1798**, sat two more summers in Reykjavík, and was then **abolished outright by royal decree on 6 June 1800.** Re-established on **8 March 1843**, it sat again on **1 July 1845** — in Reykjavík, in a school building. So not a thousand unbroken years. A thousand years with a **43-year hole** that Denmark put there.
say: the national assembly founded here in 930
the Law Rock, the cliff wall that carried the spoken law across the valley
the Law-Speaker, who recited a third of the whole legal code from memory each year
the chieftain-priests, about 36 of them, who ran it by consensus

block.title: ⚖️ Kristnitaka
block.sub: The Day Iceland Changed Religion, Lying Down
block.cue: Standing at Lögberg. This is the exact ground where it was decided.
block.hook: Around **the year 1000**, Iceland changed its national religion **without a single sword being drawn** — right here. No army. No martyrs. Just one pagan chieftain, one cloak, and a really long nap.
block.point: Most national religions are imposed by kings or won by armies. Iceland's was decided **on this rock, by a man having a lie-down.**
block.mic: Calmly, collectively, and after a really good night's sleep. That is how Iceland became Christian — standing where you are standing. Most countries were not given the option.
block.weather: Weather pivot: "Þorgeir lay under a fur cloak for a day and a night. In this, you can see why."
bullets: By **999** the country was split — Christian districts against pagan strongholds — and Norway's King **Ólafur Tryggvason** was squeezing hard: he welcomed Christian traders into his ports, barred the pagans, and **held Icelandic hostages** as leverage. Convert, or lose the trade route you cannot live without.
Persuasion had gone badly. One Saxon priest, **Þangbrandur**, allegedly **fought duels and killed poets** who mocked his sermons. Not a charm offensive.

By **AD 1000** (the sources wobble between 999 and 1000) the **Alþingi** met on this spot facing two religions, two law codes and one looming civil war — so both sides handed the verdict to one man: **Þorgeir Ljósvetningagoði**, the *pagan* Law-Speaker.

He lay down under his cloak **a full day and a night**, then stood up on this rock and ruled: **one law, one people, one faith — Christianity** — so the young commonwealth would not split in two. Private sacrifice, horse-meat and infant exposure were quietly tolerated at first, then dropped. Food is food.
say: the pagan Law-Speaker who lay under his cloak a day and a night, then chose Christianity
the Saxon priest who fought duels with the poets who mocked his sermons
Norway's king, who squeezed Iceland with port bans and hostages

block.title: ⛪ Þingvallabær & Skáldareitur
block.sub: A Westminster Abbey With Two Occupants
block.cue: The white church and the five-gabled farmhouse on your right, at the bottom of the wall.
block.hook: There has been a church on this spot since **1017**. Beside it is a **national burial ground built to hold Iceland's greatest artists** — and in eighty-five years it has managed to bury exactly **two people**.
block.point: A thousand-year-old church, a Prime Minister's summer house, and a national shrine containing two poets — one of whom may not be the right man.
block.mic: They built this to hold the greatest Icelanders who ever lived. Two people went in. Then everyone thought about it a bit more and decided, actually, we'd rather be buried at home.
block.weather: Weather pivot: "The white church against a grey sky is the photograph everybody takes anyway."
bullets: The church first went up around **1017**, the present building dates from **1859**, and the bell tower was added in **1907** — the date is on the weather vane. It has no resident priest; the one who serves it **comes out from Skálholt**, which we pass later today.

The five-gabled farmhouse beside it is **Þingvallabær**, built in **1930** for the Alþingi millennium festival by **Guðjón Samúelsson**, the state architect. He turned its face deliberately toward **Almannagjá** — the older turf farmhouse it replaced had looked out at the lake. It began with **three gables**; two more were added after a **1970 fire** destroyed the king's house next door. Since **1974** it has been the **Prime Minister's summer residence.** One gable belongs to the church.

Behind the church is **Skáldareitur**, the poets' plot — and it exists because of an argument over a corpse. When **Einar Benediktsson** died in **January 1940**, his ex-wife and his companion could not agree who had the right to bury him. **Jónas Jónsson frá Hriflu** saw the opening and proposed a national honour ground here, modelled on **Westminster Abbey**. Einar went into it on **27 January 1940**.

The second and last arrival was **Jónas Hallgrímsson**, Iceland's national poet, who had died in Copenhagen on **26 May 1845** of blood poisoning after breaking his leg on a staircase. His bones came home and were buried here on **16 November 1946** — over the objection of the man who dug them up, who wanted him in **Öxnadalur** where he was born. The Prime Minister, **Ólafur Thors**, overruled him. The government's position was that **Jónas's bones were state property.**

And nobody is sure they are his. Two other people had been buried on top of him in **1875** and **1900**, and both had to be lifted out first. The doubt has never gone away — there are still calls to open the grave and test what is in it.

Two graves. That is the whole national pantheon. **Halldór Laxness**, whose house we passed this morning, is not here. **Kjarval**, who opened this tour, is not here either. Iceland built itself a Westminster Abbey and then quietly stopped using it.
say: the five-gabled farmhouse, the Prime Minister's summer residence
the church, on this spot since 1017
the poets' plot behind the church
the poet whose disputed funeral created the place, buried 1940
the state architect who built the farmhouse in 1930

block.title: 💧 Öxarárfoss, Drekkingarhylur & Peningagjá
block.sub: The Waterfall, the Drowning Pool and the Fake Wishing Well
block.cue: Follow the Öxará. The waterfall ahead, the still green pool below it, and the coin-filled crack by the bridge.
block.hook: A waterfall that was **moved here on purpose**, a pool where **at least eighteen women were drowned**, and a wishing well invented by **a sign put up in the 1930s.**
block.point: The law was spoken up on the rock. It was carried out down here, in the water.
block.mic: People throw coins in and make a wish because a sign in the 1930s told them to. Icelanders have been quietly watching tourists do it ever since and saying nothing.
block.weather: Weather pivot: "Rain makes the falls louder and the pool darker. Neither improves the story of this place."
bullets: The **Öxará** comes over the wall at **Öxarárfoss** and runs down through the assembly ground. It is the main open river feeding the whole valley — and it is doing a job it was very probably given, diverted to bring water to the assembly.

Below the falls the river widens into a still green pool: **Drekkingarhylur**, the drowning pool. After the Reformation Iceland adopted a severe moral code, **Stóridómur**, in **1564**, and Þingvellir doubled as an execution ground — men **beheaded, hanged or burned**; women convicted of **adultery, incest, perjury or infanticide** were **drowned here**.

Court records point to **at least eighteen women killed at this pool between about 1618 and 1749.** A memorial plaque now names them. Two weeks a year this place made the law. It also carried out the sentence.

And then there is **Peningagjá** — the crack full of coins by the bridge, properly the southern end of **Nikulásargjá**. The coins have nothing to do with the sagas. The **bridge went up in 1907** for the visit of the Danish king **Frederick VIII**, who is said to have thrown the first one in.

The wish came later, and from a signpost. In the **1930s** somebody put up a board reading **"to the wishing well"** — and that is the entire origin of the tradition. The national park's own record is blunt about it: **no older Icelandic folk tale or story about wishing here exists.** An ancient custom, ninety years old, invented by signage.
say: the waterfall coming over the rift wall
the 1564 moral code that made the drownings law
the coin crack, properly the south end of Nikulásargjá

block.title: 🐟 Þingvallavatn & Silfra
block.sub: The Cleanest Water on Earth, and Four Fish That Are One Fish
block.cue: The lake filling the rift ahead of you, and the clear pools off to the side.
block.hook: Meltwater that left a glacier **thirty to a hundred years ago**, filtered through lava the whole way — **drinkable from your cupped hand**, with **120 m** of underwater visibility. And one fish in it that has quietly become four.
block.point: Two continents pulling apart, the cleanest drinking water on the planet running through the gap, and a fish quietly turning into four other fish while nobody watches.
block.mic: Iceland's answer to a tectonic disaster: turn it into a reservoir, then drink it.
block.weather: Weather pivot: "If the far shore has gone, that is the rift you cannot see across — which is rather the point."
bullets: **Þingvallavatn** is Iceland's largest natural lake: about **84 km²**, up to **114 m deep**, averaging **34 m**, sitting at roughly **100.5 m above sea level** — and its bed lies **below sea level** because of the rifting.

About **nine-tenths of everything entering it arrives from below**, seeping up through porous lava at **3–4°C**. Only about a tenth comes in as visible surface water, most of that the **Öxará**. The catchment runs to some **1,300 km²**, of which the lake is only about **six per cent** — the rest is plumbing you cannot see.

The water begins as snow on **Langjökull** and spends **thirty to a hundred years** underground before it surfaces. Clear pools like **Silfra** are that meltwater arriving. The water in front of you fell before some of you were born.

In that lake, one Arctic charr arrived after the ice left and split into **four separate forms in about 10,000 years.** **Kuðungableikja**, the snail charr. **Dvergbleikja**, the dwarf. **Murta**, the small open-water one. **Sílableikja**, the fish-eater. Two feed on the bottom, two feed in open water — and they are **all one species**, *Salvelinus alpinus*. They can interbreed and produce fertile young. They largely decline to.

**Three of the four are genetically distinct.** The fourth, sílableikja, comes out muddled — some read as murta, others as crosses. Vísindavefurinn's assessment is that this may be **sympatric speciation**, one population dividing with no physical barrier between the halves, and that another **10,000 years** could produce genuinely separate species. Evolution has not finished tidying up.

That island out in the lake is **Sandey**, a **tuff cone** built by **Hengill** about **1,900 years ago** — the same eruption that laid down **Nesjahraun** at the north end. An eruption happened in the middle of a lake and built itself an island out of it.
say: Iceland's largest natural lake, filling the rift floor
the clear pool you can drink from, visibility up to 120 m
the glacier the water left 30 to 100 years ago
the small open-water charr, one of the lake's four forms
the tuff-cone island Hengill built about 1,900 years ago

block.title: 🇮🇸 17 June 1944
block.cue: Back at the Law Rock. This is where the country stopped belonging to anybody else.
block.hook: On **17 June 1944** Iceland declared itself a republic — not in the capital, but **here**, in the rain, in front of tens of thousands of people standing in this valley.
block.point: A thousand years after the first assembly, on the same ground, the country finished the job.
block.mic: It absolutely poured. Tens of thousands stood in it for hours. If you want one image of how much this particular field means to Icelanders — that is the one.
block.weather: Weather pivot: "It poured on the day itself. Thousands stood in it anyway."
bullets: They could have done it in Reykjavík, in a building, dry. They chose this ground instead: **the place the nation first assembled in 930**, and the place Denmark had shut down in **1800**.
The date was not an accident either — **17 June** is the birthday of **Jón Sigurðsson**, the man who led the independence campaign and who did not live to see it.
It rained. It rained hard, the whole way through. Nobody left. The photographs of that day are mostly a valley full of soaked people refusing to go home.
say: the independence leader whose birthday, 17 June, became the national day
republic; the word they were there to say

block.title: 🕳️ The Cave People
block.cue: Driving past Laugarvatnshellir.
block.hook: The last family to call an Icelandic **cave** home moved out in **1922** — no electricity, no plumbing, but **their own front door** and a cow tied up next door.
block.point: Twentieth-century Europe had jazz, cars and radio. It also had **a family raising kids in a cave**, because that's what was available.
block.mic: Legend says a shepherd here was repeatedly **dragged out of the cave by invisible hands** — right before a blizzard that would have killed him inside. In Iceland, even the hidden folk do their own weather warnings.
block.weather: Weather pivot: "Low cloud is the right weather for this. They lived in a cave because of days like this."
bullets: **Laugarvatnshellir** is a pair of man-made caves hacked out of soft **palagonite tuff** (solidified volcanic ash) on the **Lyngdalsheiði** heath, between Þingvellir and Laugarvatn.

First in, **1910**: the carpenter **Indriði Guðmundsson** and **Guðrún Kolbeinsdóttir**, who lasted about **eleven months** and ran a **coffee-bread-and-cakes tent** for passing Golden Circle travellers — Iceland's original roadside café, carved edition.

Then **1918–1922**: **Jón Þorvarðsson** and **Vigdís Helgadóttir** raised **three children** in the rock. When a blizzard blocked the midwife, Jón **delivered his own daughter Ragnheiður** himself — cave dad of the century.
Not medieval, either: this was **the same decade as the Model T Ford**. Reopened to visitors in **2017** — original door back in place, coffee pot and all.
say: the pair of man-made caves families actually lived in until 1922
the lake village the caves are named after
the carpenter who moved in first, in 1910
the other 1910 tenant; the two of them lasted eleven months and ran a coffee tent
the father who delivered his own daughter in the cave
the mother who raised three children in the rock, 1918 to 1922
the daughter born in the cave when a blizzard blocked the midwife
the heath the caves are cut into

block.title: 🌋 Hekla
block.cue: Look right at 1 o'clock — Hekla, sixty kilometres out on the horizon. Clear days only.
block.hook: In medieval Europe, this was officially **the front door of Hell** — and the prison of **Judas Iscariot**. Iceland didn't argue. We just charged tourists.
block.point: Most volcanoes get a Wikipedia entry. Hekla got a **theological one** — used to scare medieval Europe straight for 800 years.
block.mic: Welcome to the gateway to Hell. It gives you barely **an hour and a half's notice** to send the postcards.
block.weather: Weather pivot: "Hekla is out sixty kilometres and hides most days. Medieval Europe thought that was deliberate."
bullets: **Hekla** — **1,491 m**, erupted **20+ times since the Vikings**; the **1104** blast (**VEI 5**) dropped ~**2 km³ of tephra over 55,000 km²**, one of the biggest in Iceland's record and the one that started the legend.
When word of 1104 reached Europe, **Cistercian monks** ran with it — by **1180** Herbert of Clairvaux wrote that next to Hekla, Etna was "a small furnace."
Through the 12th–13th centuries the Church named Hekla the **literal mouth of Hell** and a prison of **Judas Iscariot**.
Last erupted **February 2000** — and Hekla is so eerily quiet beforehand that seismographs picked up its run-up only about **80 minutes** before it blew.

She is a great deal older than her CV suggests. The story of the Hekla we would recognise today begins **just over 7,000 years ago** — she was already in business long before anyone was here to take notes. **1104** was her **first eruption after the settlement of Iceland** — and it is still **her own largest explosive eruption in historical time.** (The bigger explosive eruption in Iceland's historical record belongs to a rival: **Öræfajökull in 1362.**) She had been quiet for roughly **three centuries** beforehand, which means nobody then alive had the faintest idea what she was capable of.

The ash of 1104 went north, and the farming districts of **Þjórsárdalur** and **Hrunamannahreppur** were **abandoned** because of it. Iceland got a thousand years of European publicity out of that eruption and **wrote none of it** — the people actually living underneath were otherwise engaged, emptying two districts.

The Judas story has a date and a document. **Within ten to twenty years of 1104** an **English poem** was already asserting that **Judas** — the arch-traitor himself — was imprisoned inside Hekla, and European clergy positively welcomed eruption reports, because to their minds an eruption **proved that Hell existed.** The image that fixed it was a woodcut in the history of the Northern Peoples by the Swedish churchman **Olaus Magnus (1490–1557)**, published in **Venice in 1555**, showing Hekla with a set of tunnels running down out of the mountain. **Vesuvius and Etna never acquired the same reputation** — and Vísindavefur offers the driest explanation available. They were **too close to civilisation.** A volcano safely off the edge of Europe made a far more convincing front door.

Her longest eruption began on **5 April 1766** and continued with breaks until **May 1768** — **just over two years**, including a **six-month pause** in the middle that must have felt to everyone like the end of it.

On a very, very clear day this same sightline stacks up **three more ice-capped volcanoes** toward the coast: **Tindfjallajökull**, then **Eyjafjallajökull** — of 2010 ash-cloud fame — then **Mýrdalsjökull** behind it.
say: the 1,491 m volcano medieval Europe called the gateway to Hell
volcanic ash and fragments; Hekla dropped about 2 km³ of it in 1104
the first of the three glaciers visible on a very clear day
the 2010 ash-cloud volcano, second in the stack
the third glacier in the stack, furthest toward the coast

block.title: 🛁 Laugarvatn & Apavatn
block.cue: Look right at 3 o'clock — Laugarvatn lake.
block.hook: What happens when you put the leaders of an entire country into the **same hot water** to settle an argument? Iceland has been finding out for a thousand years — and the answer, twice, was **not what anybody promised.**
block.point: A country changed religion over the water temperature, and a chieftain swore an oath on a book nobody can name. Both stories are better than the tidy versions.
block.mic: Iceland converted to Christianity and then negotiated where to get wet. Honestly, that is the most Icelandic detail in the entire conversion.
block.weather: Weather pivot: "Rain actually helps this one — the steam off the shore shows up better against a grey sky."
bullets: **Laugarvatn** — "Pool Lake" — **280 people at 1 January 2026.** Hot springs feed the lake, and along parts of the shore the water genuinely runs bath-warm in mid-winter. **I am not going to give you a temperature for the lake**, because there is no single honest number: different outlets run at different heats. What *is* measured is the spring above **Vígðalaug**, which runs **up to about 90°C and often between 70 and 80** — and **Þorvaldur Thoroddsen measured 54°C** in the built pool there back in **1889.**

**Its moment came around the year 1000.** **Kristni saga** — not Íslendingabók, the two get mixed up constantly — says that once Christianity had been voted through at Þingvellir, **the northerners and the southerners were baptised at Reykjalaug in Laugardalur**, and gives the reason with beautiful bluntness: **they did not want to go into cold water.** A whole country changes religion, and the sticking point is the temperature.

**Now the part every guide gets wrong, including the version I used to tell.** The pool you can walk to today is called **Vígðalaug**, the Consecrated Pool — but **Kristni saga never renames anything.** It says Reykjalaug and stops. **Kålund** described the pool in **1873** without identifying it as the baptism site at all; **Thoroddsen** in **1889** wrote only that Reykjalaug was *probably* at Laugarvatn and that **certainty was lacking**; and the identification of *this* pool with *that* text appears **not to have been made until the twentieth century.** A **1999 excavation found no tephra and nothing datable** — archaeologically, it **cannot** be dated to the year 1000.
So: a real pool, a real text, a tradition joining them that is about a hundred years old. **That is still a good story. It is just not the same story as a fact.**

**Next door is Apavatn — "Marsh Lake" — and this is where the cold politics happened.** In the **spring of 1238**, **Sturla Sighvatsson** did not ambush **Gizur Þorvaldsson** out of nowhere: he **summoned him**, and Gizur came with **forty selected men.** Sturla said he meant no betrayal, and then **had the lot of them seized and disarmed by force.**

**A book was brought out** — the saga says *bók*, and **it does not say Bible** — and Gizur swore on it: **to sail abroad, and to keep faith with Sturla.** Note what is *not* in the oath: **he never swore to give up power.** That was handled separately, when **Hjalti Magnússon** took over his **goðorð**.
**Gizur broke it anyway.** What happened five months later is the next block, and it is the worst afternoon in Icelandic history.
Today Laugarvatn has the **Fontana** baths on the same shore — the same warmth that decided a national conversion, now with a bar.
say: "Pool Lake", 280 people, warm along parts of the shore
"Marsh Lake" next door, where Gizur was seized in the spring of 1238
the name Kristni saga actually gives the baptism spring
"the Consecrated Pool", the name the surviving pool carries today
the Sturlungar chief who summoned Gizur and then took him
the Haukdælir rival who swore on a book and broke it
a chieftaincy; the thing Gizur actually lost, and not in the oath
the baths on that shore today
