block.title: 💙 Brúará
block.sub: The River That Lost Its Bridge
block.cue: Crossing Brúará.
block.hook: A river whose name literally means **"Bridge-River"** — except the bridge was a **natural stone arch**, and in **1602** the church **smashed it on purpose** to keep the starving out.
block.point: A river named after a bridge — that lost the bridge because the church was tired of the poor arriving.
block.mic: The cheapest border policy in Icelandic history: knock down the only bridge and let the river do the rest.
block.weather: Weather pivot: "Rivers do not need good weather. This one is loudest when the sky is worst."
bullets: **Brúará** ("Bridge-River") is a clear, spring-fed river feeding the Hvítá; its showpiece is the electric-blue waterfall **Brúarfoss**. For centuries a natural **stone arch** here was the only crossing for miles.

In the famine year **1602**, the steward of **Skálholt** — the great church estate on today's route — with the knowledge of the bishop's wife, **Helga Jónsdóttir**, had the arch **deliberately destroyed** to stop displaced, starving people crossing to reach the estate's fertile land. Charity, Skálholt-style: demolish the bridge so the hungry can't walk over it.
The river had form: back in **1433** the disgraced bishop **Jón Gerreksson** was **drowned in it in a sack** as an execution. Not a lucky river to owe a bishop money.
say: "Bridge-River", the clear spring-fed river we are crossing
the bishop's wife who knew the stone arch was being destroyed in 1602
the disgraced bishop drowned here in a sack in 1433
the church estate whose steward had the arch smashed

block.title: ⚖️ The Sturlung Age
block.sub: The Civil War That Ended the Republic
block.cue: *The 13th-century chapter most tours skip.*
block.hook: Iceland governed itself without a king for three hundred years. Then a handful of families decided that was inefficient — and **burned the whole arrangement down.** Literally, in one case, with the wedding guests still inside.
block.point: A republic that lasted three centuries was finished off by six men in a cellar, a bending spear, and a document nobody can produce the original of.
block.mic: The most famous last words in Icelandic history are "do not strike" — and he had to say them twice.
block.weather: Weather pivot: "This one needs no window at all. Close your eyes if you like; it is better in the dark anyway."
bullets: The **Sturlungaöld** is usually dated from **about 1220 to 1262** — **Sögufélag says 1264**, because the submission to Norway went **district by district** rather than all at once. Iceland's longest and ugliest internal war.

Power had pooled into a few big clans, above all the **Sturlungar** — the family of the saga-writer **Snorri Sturluson**. Disputes stopped going to the Althing and started going to **swords, fires and assassinations**.

**Spring 1238, at Apavatn** — the lake we just passed. **Sturla Sighvatsson summoned Gizur Þorvaldsson**, who came with **forty picked men**. Sturla swore he meant nothing by it, then **had them all seized and disarmed.** A **book** was produced — the saga says *bók*, not Bible — and Gizur swore **to sail abroad and keep faith**. He did neither.

**Five months later, on 21 August 1238, they met at Örlygsstaðir.** Be honest about the numbers, because the tidy version is wrong: **Íslendinga saga gives shifting totals** as forces joined and split — Gizur and **Kolbeinn ungi** with **1,300** at one point, about **1,300** again at Reykjarlaug, then **Brandur arriving with another hundred**, against **four hundred with Sighvatur** and others besides. A modern Icelandic reconstruction puts it at **more than 1,600 against more than 1,200.** It is **often described as the most populous battle ever fought on Icelandic soil** — and I will give you that description, but **nobody has ever demonstrated it.**

**Sturla's spear has a name and a problem.** **Grásíða** was **large, old, and not very stiff**: he thrust so hard that men went down in front of him, but **the spear kept bending, and he had to put it under his foot to straighten it** between attacks. A family heirloom, failing in real time, in the middle of the worst afternoon of his life.

**How he died is not one blow, and the saga is specific.** **Húnröður Magnússon** stabbed him through the right cheek. **Hjalti Magnússon** through the left cheek and the tongue. **Böðvar kappi** into the throat. **Gizur** then struck a great axe wound **behind the left ear**. **Klængur Bjarnarson** thrust into the wound already in his throat. **Markús Marðarson** stabbed his belly. **The text names no single fatal blow** — so when you hear that Gizur killed him, that is a summary of a queue.

**Snorri Sturluson — the man who wrote down Norse mythology — was killed at Reykholt on the night of 23 September 1241.** King **Hákon** had sent a letter demanding he come to Norway and answer for himself; **Gizur Þorvaldsson**, his own former son-in-law, brought **seventy men**. **Five went down into the cellar**: Markús Marðarson, Símon knútur, Árni beiskur, Þorsteinn Guðinason and Þórarinn Ásgrímsson. **Símon told Árni to strike.** Snorri said **"Eigi skal höggva"** — *do not strike* — **and the saga records that he said it twice.** They struck. (Íslendinga saga, chapter 156.)

**The low point was the Burning of Flugumýri, 22 October 1253** — a wedding ambush, the hall fired with the family inside. It is often compared to a certain television wedding; that comparison is a modern one and I will label it as such.

**And the ending is messier than the textbook.** Beginning in **1262** and finished by **1264**, the districts accepted the King of Norway one by one. The document we call **Gamli sáttmáli** records the conditions — but **no original signed 1262 treaty survives.** The manuscript it comes down in, **AM 45 8vo**, is a **damaged law book written in the second half of the sixteenth century**, and Sagnfræðistofnun at the University of Iceland suggests the text is better read as **a homage document, a list of conditions**, than as a treaty between two parties. **Three hundred years of self-government ended, and we cannot produce the paperwork.**
say: the Sturlung Age, about 1220 to 1262, or 1264 if you count the finish
who wrote down Norse mythology and died in his own cellar
the part of Sturlunga that tells all of this; chapter 156 for the cellar
who broke the oath, won, and led the party to Reykholt
"Grey-flank", the old spear he had to straighten under his foot
the hall burned with the wedding party inside, 22 October 1253
"the Old Covenant", surviving only in a 16th-century law book

block.title: ⚖️ Haukadalur
block.cue: At the geothermal field of Haukadalur.
block.hook: One farm in this steaming valley bred a **dynasty**: the first bishop's family, the household that raised the man who wrote Iceland's memory down — and the one who **ended the republic**. Meet the **Haukdælir**.
block.point: One valley, one family: the first bishop's line, the household that preserved Iceland's memory — and the earl who signed the republic away.
block.mic: The hawks of this valley taught Iceland to write its own history down. Then one of them handed the country to a foreign king, which is a hell of a way to end a family story.
block.weather: Weather pivot: "Steam and low cloud look identical from here. Both mean the ground is warm."
bullets: **Haukadalur** reads as **"Valley of the Hawks"** — *haukur*, hawk, and *dalur*, valley — though I will be straight with you: **that is the obvious reading, not a documented etymology.** Nobody has proved that is where the name came from.
Known now for steam, but for two centuries this was a **chieftain's seat**: the home farm of the **Haukdælir**, one of the great power families of the Icelandic Commonwealth.

**Teitur Ísleifsson** — son of **Ísleifur Gissurarson, Iceland's first bishop** — is the man the family line runs through, and this valley held **a learned household**, not a school in any modern sense. (The *school* crown belongs to **Skálholt**, down the road.)

**And here is what it produced.** **Ari fróði Þorgilsson** — "the Wise", **1068 to 1148** — **came to Haukadalur at the age of seven and stayed fourteen winters.** He grew up to write **Íslendingabók**, between **1122 and 1132** — the reason Iceland has any firm early dates at all. **A boy was sent to a farm in a steaming valley, and the country got its memory.**

The family stayed at the top for two centuries — bishops, lawmen, and finally **Gizur Þorvaldsson**, the oath-breaker of Örlygsstaðir: a **Haukdæling**, and in **1258** the Norwegian king made him **jarl — earl** — of Iceland, though at first **only over some districts and with his authority unclear.** Four years later the republic he had helped bury was handed to Norway.

**The valley also holds Geysir and Strokkur** — the original *geysir*, the Icelandic verb *að geysa*, to gush, which gave the word to every language that has one. Geologically it is the **Geysir high-temperature geothermal field, on the eastern margin of Iceland's Western Volcanic Zone** — a **borderline field**, in the literature's own phrase. (I used to say "the Hreppar block". The Hreppar **microplate** is real, and it is real regional context between the two volcanic zones — but it is not the description of this field, so I have stopped using it here.)

**And be honest about the star turn: Geysir is dormant.** It woke up briefly after the earthquakes of **2000** and its **last known eruptions were in 2016.** The one you are going to watch is **Strokkur** — and its interval is **not** "every five minutes" either: the monitoring study gives an **observed range of 3.7 to 16.4 minutes.** Point your camera and be patient. It owes you nothing.
say: the steaming valley; haukur hawk, dalur valley
the dynasty out of it: bishops, a learned household, and one earl
the bishop's son the family line runs through
"the Wise", 1068–1148, who came here aged seven and stayed fourteen winters
the original hot spring that gave every language the word geyser; dormant, last known eruptions 2016
"the Churn", the one that still goes; monitored interval 3.7 to 16.4 minutes

block.title: ⛲ Geysir
block.cue: At the geothermal field — Strokkur and Geysir.
block.hook: Iceland gave the world the word **"geyser"** — from one hot spring, in one field, on one farm.
block.point: Every other geyser on the planet is named after **this one**. Yellowstone, New Zealand, Chile — all geological cousins of one Icelandic hot spring.
block.mic: Iceland exported the word "geyser" before it exported the cod.
block.weather: Weather pivot: "Wind decides which way you get soaked. Stand upwind of Strokkur and watch everyone else learn that."
bullets: The original **Geysir** is first recorded in **1294**, when earthquakes reshaped the field's springs — at its peak it threw water **60–80 m** up. **It is dormant: its last known eruptions were in 2016.** The one you are here for is its cousin **Strokkur** ("the Churn"), **15–20 m** high and occasionally 40 — and its interval is **not** the five minutes everyone quotes. The monitoring study gives an **observed range of 3.7 to 16.4 minutes.**
Watch the **dome** bulge just before it fires: a thin layer of cooler water over near-boiling water below, pressure building until it punches through.

Geologically this is the **Geysir high-temperature geothermal field, on the eastern margin of Iceland's Western Volcanic Zone** — the literature's own word for it is a **borderline field**. Water seeps down, hits **200°C+ rock**, flashes to steam and comes back up. (I used to say "the Hreppar block" here. The Hreppar **microplate** is real and it is the regional context between the two volcanic zones — but it is not the name of this field.)

The name **Geysir** (from *geysa*, "to gush") first appears in writing in **1647** — and as Enlightenment scientists took an interest, the word spread to **every language on Earth**, all from this one field.

**Geysir runs on earthquakes.** Born in the annals after the **1294** quakes, it roars back after every big southern shake — **1630**, **1896**, then **June 2000** — and dozes off again between them, sometimes for decades. **It stirred twice more in early 2016**, which is the last anybody has recorded, and the experts were quick to say that did not mean it was back.

Icelanders never quite accepted the naps: they used to **shovel rocks and turf in** to provoke it, and from **1963 to 1981** the official trick was **soap** — lower the surface tension and the superheated water boils over. The country literally **washed its geyser into performing**. (We've since let it sleep with dignity.)
At its most active it took **8 to 10 hours** to refill between eruptions. In **1896** it came back erupting **several times a day**, then fell dormant around **1915**.
A **channel was cut in 1935** to lower the water surface and restart it, then **re-cut and deepened in 1981**.

**Strokkur** is straight thermodynamics: **one metre down the water is 90–95°C**, at **ten metres 112°C**, and at the bottom of the **23-metre shaft about 130°C** — held liquid only by the weight of water above it. Take the lid off and it flashes to steam.
Measured eruptions in **2000** threw between about **270 and 425 litres** of water, or **300 to 500 litres** once you count what leaves as steam.

**Strokkur's** reliability is younger than most of its audience. Its nineteenth-century performances are said to have **lasted an hour and reached up to 60 metres** — then it fell silent for decades. In **1963** the decision was taken to **drill about 40 metres into the gosskál**, the eruption basin, and it has been **extraordinarily active** ever since. The most dependable natural spectacle in this country is not entirely natural.

One more number for the shaft: a **cold vein comes in at about 13 metres** down. That is part of why height, duration and interval all vary — and why nobody will ever hand you a timetable, so keep looking at the water rather than at your phone.
say: the original hot spring that gave every language the word geyser; dormant, last known eruptions 2016
"the Churn", the one that still goes; monitored interval 3.7 to 16.4 minutes

block.title: 💧 Hvítá & Gullfoss
block.sub: Meltwater and the Falls One Woman Saved
block.cue: At Gullfoss.
block.hook: In **1907** an investor tried to dam this waterfall — and a farmer's daughter, **Sigríður**, fought it all the way to Reykjavík. She **lost in court** — and the falls are still here anyway.
block.point: The world's most famous Icelandic conservation story — lost in the courtroom, saved in the end, by a woman who never had a vote.
block.mic: An investor showed up with engineers. A farmer's daughter showed up and lost every legal round — and the falls are still here.
block.weather: Weather pivot: "Rain makes it bigger, spray makes it wetter, and the rainbow needs sun. Two out of three today."
bullets: **Gullfoss** ("Golden Falls") drops the **Hvítá** down two staircase tiers, **32 m** total, in a narrow canyon — spray throwing rainbows so consistently it looks staged.
The Hvítá is **glacial meltwater** from **Langjökull**, silt-laden enough to glow gold in summer light.

In **1907** an Englishman leased the falls from farmer **Tómas Tómasson** for a **hydro plant**. His daughter **Sigríður Tómasdóttir** spent her own savings on a Reykjavík lawyer — **Sveinn Björnsson**, later Iceland's **first president** — and fought for years to void the lease. The famous "walked barefoot to Reykjavík / threatened to jump" details are **romanticised**; she genuinely **lost in court**, but the lease then **lapsed because the developers stopped paying the rent**.
Gullfoss survived, became a **nature reserve in 1979**, and Sigríður — remembered on a memorial above the falls — is now called **Iceland's first environmentalist**.
The gorge below runs about **2.5 km long and 70 m deep**, and mean flow over the lip is **109 m³/s**.

The Englishman's offer, early in **1907**, was **50,000 krónur** — and Iceland passed a law that same year restricting **foreign ownership of waterfalls**, after which foreign parties obtained rental rights anyway.

**Sigríður Tómasdóttir**, **1871 to 1957**, came from the farm **Brattholt** above the falls, and what she spent years trying to void were the agreements **her own father had signed**. The judgement went against the Brattholt family.

What actually saved it was duller than the legend: in **1928** the rental payments stopped and the agreement fell void. The reserve declaration was signed on **9 March 1979** and covers **164.2 hectares**.
Her lawyer was **Sveinn Björnsson**, who went on to become Iceland's first president, **1944 to 1952**. (Losing that case turned out to be quite good for his CV.)

🎬 **On screen:** Gullfoss shows up in *Vikings* (later seasons) and Netflix's *Lost in Space* — and it's the "Argentina" in the *Smallville* episode "Zod" (2006), where the final shot is captioned *Iguazú Falls* but is pure Gullfoss.
say: Golden Falls, the two-tier 32 m drop in front of you
the glacial river that falls over it
the farmer's daughter who fought the dam, and is now called Iceland's first environmentalist
her Reykjavík lawyer, later Iceland's first president
the glacier whose meltwater feeds the Hvítá

block.title: 🎧 Music Leg
block.cue: Leaving Ytri-Tunga, last stop of the day. Playlist on, mic live between the stops.
block.hook: Forty-three tracks in three acts, and the whole story of how a country with fewer people than most cities ended up on everybody's playlist. We get through the first two today.
block.point: The exact moment a country stops importing pop and starts exporting it — and you can hear it happen.
block.mic: Everything from here is Icelandic. Listen out around track twenty-one: that is this small, cold, sheep-heavy island going from copying everybody to being copied.
bullets: **ACT I — Borrowed clothes.** Iceland still working out who it sounds like. Five of the biggest singalongs here are secretly Anglo-American hits in Icelandic disguise — *Mambo Italiano*, *California Dreamin'*, *I Will*, Ray Sharpe rockabilly, and a Brita Borg banger out of Stockholm. The mambo arrived secondhand, via 1950s Manhattan. Post-war crooners, dancehall ballads, and Keflavík kids who saw The Beatles in Bournemouth and ran home to start a band.

**01 · Jeg vil ha' morfor med mig ud på sjov** — *Raquel Rastenni*. Plot twist — the Danes nicked it. The song is actually “Jag ska' ta' morfar med mej ut i kväll,” a 1949 Brita Borg banger out of Stockholm, dressed up in a Danish coat a year later. Same writers (Peter Spar / Jessup Sandy), different *morfar*.  [Secret-cover thread]

**02 · Litla flugan** — *Sigfús Halldórsson*. Iceland's most beloved earworm started as a bar bet. December 1951, Reykhólar farm — the manager Sigurður Elíasson tells Sigfús he can't turn that poem into a tune in ten minutes. Ten minutes later: a national standard. Drinks were *not* on Sigurður.

**03 · Ísland farsælda frón** — *Karlakór Reykjavíkur*. The melody Icelanders actually sing is the wrong one. Helgi Helgason's tune gets the credit — but the version everyone knows is centuries older, a Lydian-mode chant from medieval manuscripts that got married to Jónas Hallgrímsson's 1835 lyric long after the wedding bells. A 600-year-old tune wearing 19th-century words.
**04 · Bláu augun** — *Haukur Morthens*

**05 · Vor við flóann** — *Ragnar Bjarnason*. Two-for-one. The 1959 7″ gives you Ragnar singing “Vor við flóann” on the A-side — flip it over and **Guðbergur Auðunsson** takes the mic for “Hvítir svanir.” Same record, two singers, no warning.  [Recorded somewhere unusual]

**06 · Æskuminning** — *Alfreð Clausen*. 1953. Iceland's first-ever ballad recorded with a full orchestra, Carl Billich on the baton. Walked it into the SKT dance-song competition the year before — and *lost*. The audience promptly overruled the judges and handed it the people's prize. Iceland figuring out who runs music: the people. Always the people.

**07 · Lilla Jóns** — *Guðbergur Auðunsson*. It's a Ray Sharpe rockabilly tune in Icelandic drag. Jón Sigurðsson took the American melody, dressed it in his own words, and out came “Little Jónsi.”  [Secret-cover thread]

**08 · Hæ Mambó** — *Haukur Morthens*. Yes — *that* Mambo Italiano. The Rosemary Clooney one. Loftur Guðmundsson Icelanded the lyrics and Reykjavík caught the mambo bug secondhand via 1950s Manhattan.  [Secret-cover thread]
**09 · Sveitapiltsins draumur** — *Hljómar*. California Dreamin'. With Icelandic lyrics. About a country boy. Yes, really.  [Secret-cover thread]

**10 · Sveitin milli sanda** — *Elly Vilhjálms*. There are no lyrics. None. Elly sings the entire thing on one open vowel — wordless, weightless, pure *Aaaaaa*. It started life as the score to a 1962 Ósvaldur Knudsen documentary; Magnús Blöndal Jóhannsson never bothered to add words and nobody ever asked.

**11 · Vor í Vaglaskógi** — *Vilhjálmur Vilhjálmsson*. Akureyri, February 1966. Two lovers go camping in Vaglaskógur — a 300-hectare birch forest in Fnjóskadalur — and Iceland gets its forever-song. The hook line every Icelander mouths on first beat: *Draumar þess rætast, sem gistir Vaglaskóg* — “the dreams of those who sleep in Vaglaskógur come true.” Kaleo dragged it onto the global stage in 2016. The forest has not stopped collecting tourists since.

**12 · Kling Klang** — *Dátar*. 1966 Keflavík teen-rock — fine. But the keyboard player? **Þórir Baldursson.** Twelve years later he'd be playing organ on Donna Summer, Giorgio Moroder and ABBA records. Pop is a small world. Iceland is an even smaller one.

**13 · If you knew** — *Thor's Hammer*. Recorded on Parlophone — *the Beatles' label* — in London, 1966. The “Umbarumbamba” EP that houses it now goes for thousands at auction; among 60s garage-rock collectors it's the white whale, the holy grail, the EP they'll remortgage their flat for.

**14 · Tætum og tryllum** — *Stuðmenn*. From the soundtrack of *Með allt á hreinu* (1982) — Iceland's biggest film of all time. 120,000 tickets. In a country of 230,000. Half the country watched it. Half the dialogue was improvised on the day, and the rival on-screen girl-band “Gærurnar” was actually Grýlurnar (skip ahead to track 19) — meaning the battle of the bands was real on screen *and* in the bar afterwards.

**ACT II — Finding the voice.** Iceland stops borrowing and starts getting copied. *Með allt á hreinu* eats half the country's box office — **120,000 tickets, 230,000 people**. Grýlurnar weaponise punk, and the band rivalry becomes the actual plot of the film. The Sugarcubes go global. Björk goes solo. GusGus turn out to be a twelve-person filmmaking collective who picked up instruments halfway through.

**15 · Reyndu aftur** — *Magnús Eiríksson, Mannakorn*. Track 2 of Mannakorn's January 1977 sophomore LP *Í gegnum tíðina*. The voice you're hearing? Pálmi Gunnarsson — same Pálmi who'd open Iceland's Eurovision account in Bergen 1986. Track 21 is also him. The man gets around.

**16 · Skólaball** — *Brimkló*. Plot twist confirmed by RÚV in 2021: *Skólaball er um stúlku sem síðar varð konan mín* — “the girl in the song became my wife.” Magnús Kjartansson met her at an actual school dance and wrote the actual song. The most romantic Reykjavík origin story that doesn't involve a horse.  [Song about someone]

**17 · Gáta dagsins** — *Spilverk þjóðanna*. Twenty seconds. *Twenty.* “Today's Riddle” clocks in shorter than a cigarette break — a deliberately cryptic micro-piece slipped in among the album's full-length songs. Blink and you've missed it.

**18 · Á Sprengisandi** — *Þú og ég*. A 19th-century Grímur Thomsen *ghost poem* turned into a 1980 disco track. Yes. The placename comes from *sprengja* — “to ride a horse to death” — because the highland route was so brutal travellers were said to kill their mounts crossing it. Now picture that on a glitterball.  [Debut-LP opener]

**19 · Sísi** — *Grýlurnar*. It's not about anyone. The whole song is laughter and “vo-oh-oh”s and the name “Sísí” chanted as a hook — pure rhythm, no narrative. From *Mávastellið*, 1983. (The band's name means “the Grýlas” — Iceland's child-eating troll-mother, the lady who shows up at Christmas to scare your kids straight. Sweet branding.)  [Song about someone]

**20 · Svart-hvíta hetjan mín** — *Dúkkulísurnar*. Forty years and she still won't crack. Gréta Sigurjónsdóttir wrote both words and music in 1986 and Icelanders have been begging ever since: *who is the black-and-white hero?* Not telling. “Their best-kept secret.” Stop asking.  [Song about someone]

**21 · Þorparinn** — *Magnús Eiríksson, Pálmi Gunnarsson*. The song is about its own singer. Magnús Eiríksson watched his friend Pálmi Gunnarsson hauling fish in Vopnafjörður before fame found him — and wrote it down. The voice you're hearing is the voice of the song's own subject. Meta-loop activated.  [Song about someone]

**22 · Deus** — *The Sugarcubes*. “Deus does not exist… but if he does, he lives in the sky above me.” Sing-songed like a kindergarten chant. Delivered in fluent Icelandic blasphemy. Whole band straight-faced through the entire thing. The Sugarcubes never did anything halfway.

**23 · Venus As A Boy – 7″ Dream Mix** — *Björk, Mick Hucknall, Gota Yashiki*. Now for the most-WTF production credit on this entire playlist — the 1993 “Dream Mix” was produced by **Mick Hucknall.** As in: Simply Red. As in: *Holding Back the Years* Mick Hucknall. He had a side production company called Dream that year and Björk used it. Pop is so weird.

**24 · Lög unga fólksins** — *Unun*. Title nicked straight from RÚV — *Lög unga fólksins* is Iceland's long-running pop-request show, “Songs of Young People.” Naming your 1994 alt-rock single after the state-broadcast request show is the indie equivalent of calling your album *Top of the Pops*.

**25 · Oh – Edit** — *GusGus*. Hidden inside this slick Reykjavík club banger: a 1959 *tiki-bar* instrumental. Hawaiian exotica composer Arthur Lyman's “Taboo Tu,” sampled in. GusGus reached back forty years and pulled out a luau.

**26 · Sá ég spóa** — *Savanna tríóið*. Authorship: nobody. It's a *þjóðlag* — an anonymous Icelandic folk song that Savanna tríóið nailed down in the now-definitive arrangement. The lyric is twelve seconds of pocket-sized natural history: a curlew on the marsh, a golden plover singing “bí-bí-bí,” and that's it — that's spring, officially clocked in by the *lóa*.

**27 · Serenade** — *Emilíana Torrini*. Album closer of *Fisherman's Woman* (Rough Trade, 2005). Torrini said the entire album was “a letter I wrote to a person that I lost at that time. I coped by thinking I was with a fisherman.” Serenade is the dream-state final page of that letter — the bit where she lets him go.

block.title: ⚡ Tungufljót
block.sub: The Quiet Tributary & Brú Power Plant
block.cue: Crossing the Tungufljót river.
block.hook: A river you've never heard of, **powering a country you have** — quietly.
block.point: Iceland's most-photographed waterfall is Gullfoss. Its most useful one is **this tributary you're crossing**, doing the actual work of keeping the lights on.
block.mic: Gullfoss gets the photos. Tungufljót gets the electricity bill paid.
block.weather: Weather pivot: "A working river in working weather. It does not stop for either of us."
bullets: **Tungufljót** ("Tongue-River") drains the highlands into the **Hvítá**, and its showpiece is **Faxi** (Vatnsleysufoss) — a broad, low **~7 m** curtain of a waterfall with a **salmon ladder** built into it.

Its water now spins **Brúárvirkjun**, a small **Landsvirkjun** hydro station damming the upper river — a modern plant opened in the early **2020s**. Tiny globally; big enough to help keep this stretch of the south on the grid.
Iceland runs on **~70% hydro** plus geothermal — a grid that's **~99.9% renewable**, one of the cleanest on Earth. Quiet little rivers like this are the majority behind that number.
say: Tongue-River, the quiet river we're crossing
Vatnsleysufoss, its broad 7 m curtain of a waterfall with a salmon ladder built in
the small hydro station its water now spins
the glacial river this one drains into

block.title: 🍅 Reykholt & Friðheimar
block.cue: Passing Friðheimar, Reykholt.
block.hook: Iceland grows **tomatoes, cucumbers, peppers and strawberries** a shade south of the latitude of **Fairbanks, Alaska** — and the heating bill is a hole in the ground.
block.point: Just south of the Arctic you shouldn't be able to grow a tomato — so Iceland grows a big share of its own on volcano heat and skips the shipping.
block.mic: At our latitude you shouldn't be able to grow a tomato. So we built a farm on a volcano, lit it with a waterfall, and imported bees to run it.
block.weather: Weather pivot: "The greenhouses do not care what the sky is doing. That is the entire business model."
bullets: **Reykholt** ("smoky hill") in **Bláskógabyggð** is the village; **Friðheimar** is its headline farm, a working greenhouse where you eat lunch **among the vines**, soup ladled three feet from the plant that grew it. And the village is booming — **474 people on 1 January 2026**, up from **321 three years before**. Grow tomatoes, apparently, and people follow.

The heat comes out of the ground **200 metres away** and arrives in the houses at **about 95°C**. The glass is only **4 mm** thick — you want every scrap of daylight, so you accept the heat loss — and the place therefore drinks roughly **200,000 tonnes of hot water a year**. The source is **Reykholtshver**, an old geyser that still erupts about **every ten minutes** and delivers **14 litres a second at 100°C**, heating the village's houses and glass alike.

Here's the bit most guides get wrong: **geothermal gives you heat, not light.** At this latitude the sun effectively resigns in November, so the plants run on **grow-lights powered by hydro**, and **CO₂ drawn from natural geothermal steam** is piped in to speed up photosynthesis. Volcano heats it, waterfall lights it, volcano feeds it. Heat **plus** light, never heat alone.

The hardest-working department is one nobody applies to: about **1,200 bumblebees**, a species brought into Iceland specifically to pollinate greenhouses. Each can work **around 2,000 flowers a day** in good conditions — and it needs to, because there are **25,000 plants** in there, every one of them opening two to four fresh flowers a day. No sick days, no HR complaints, paid entirely in pollen.

The output is **up to two tonnes of tomatoes a day**, every day of the year. About **5%** come out scratched, undersized or misshapen — those go straight into the kitchen behind you, which is the real reason the soup exists. Even the green ones left on the plants at changeover get used. Nothing is thrown away.

**Knútur Rafn Ármann** and **Helena Hermundardóttir** bought the place in **1995**: two greenhouses and a big farmhouse nobody had lived in for years, though there had been growing under glass here since **1946**. In **2008** they opened the farm to visitors as a small sideline. Today **tourism is two thirds of the turnover** and the tomatoes are one third, with **110 year-round staff** and another 15–20 in summer. The sideline ate the business.

They are still building. **17,000 m² of glass**, of which **6,000 m²** has already swapped the old sodium lamps for **LED** — about **half the electricity** — and the rest follows by **2028**. In **2025** they took over **Jarðarberjaland** next door, Iceland's strawberry specialist, and are taking it from **3,600 to 6,000 m²**, lifting it from **60 tonnes of strawberries a year to 100**. Icelandic strawberries are still only **three to four percent** of the market, so there is room to grow.

None of this is new here. Iceland's **first geothermally heated greenhouses went up at Reykir in Mosfellssveit in 1924** — three of them in a single spring and summer — and that is the year the whole industry dates from. The **first greenhouse in Biskupstungur came in 1932**, built at Reykholt by the local schoolmaster, **Stefán Sigurðsson**. Down the road, **Espiflöt** has been going since **1948** and now grows flowers only. And the **very first greenhouse in Iceland**, at Sauðárkrókur in the late 1890s, was heated by **fermenting horse manure** — so on balance, the volcano was an upgrade.
say: "smoky hill", the greenhouse village we are passing
its tomato farm, where you eat lunch among the vines
the geyser that heats the village and the greenhouses
literally "strawberry land", the strawberry house Friðheimar took over in 2025

block.title: 🐎 Icelandic Horses
block.cue: Look at the horses in the field.
block.hook: The horse in that field is a **direct descendant of a Viking horse** — a bloodline effectively **closed for ~1,000 years**. Just don't call it a pony. That's the one hill Iceland will genuinely die on.
block.point: A horse breed Vikings would still recognise — kept intact for a millennium by isolation, hard winters, and a one-way export door.
block.mic: You can take an Icelandic horse out of Iceland. You just can't bring it back. The country runs a one-way door for its own livestock.
block.weather: Weather pivot: "They will be standing in it, tails to the wind, entirely unbothered. Take the lesson."
bullets: The **Icelandic horse** is small (**~132–145 cm**), shaggy, long-lived (often **30 years**), tough and frankly opinionated — and by breed convention and national insistence, **always a "horse," never a pony**.

No new bloodstock has arrived since roughly the year **1000**, so it's essentially a **closed, disease-naïve population** — one of the purest native breeds on Earth. Tradition says the **Alþingi** slammed the import door around **982**; the documented ban dates to **1882** — and it still stands.

Most breeds have three or four gaits; the Icelandic has up to **five**, including the famous **tölt** — a four-beat running walk so smooth you could carry a full beer and not spill it. The extra gaits trace to a **single gene mutation**.

Population ~**78,000** in Iceland and ~**195,000 abroad** across 30+ countries — the diaspora outnumbers the home herd two to one, and **not one of them is ever allowed back** (biosecurity enforced by MAST, the food and veterinary authority).
say: the smooth four-beat running walk you could carry a full beer through

block.title: ⛪ Skálholt
block.cue: At Skálholt.
block.hook: For **700 years**, this farm was Iceland's **capital, university and cathedral** rolled into one. Then a **1784 earthquake** ate the lot — and the country never gave it back.
block.point: Iceland's centre of power didn't fall to an invasion. It fell to a fault line — and politics finished the job.
block.mic: A 700-year capital, ended by a single earthquake and a Danish administrative form.
block.weather: Weather pivot: "Grey and windswept is how this place looked for most of its eight hundred years."
bullets: **Skálholt** was Iceland's first **episcopal see**, founded **1056** — for 700 years the country's brain: bishops, Iceland's **first school** — **Skálholtsskóli**, a school from Ísleifur's time — a scriptorium and a library, all bankrolled by a guaranteed **church tithe from 1097**.

It gave Iceland its **only saint** — **Þorlákur Þórhallsson**, declared holy by the Alþingi in **1198** and formally made **patron saint of Iceland by the Vatican in 1984**; his feast on 23 December still anchors the Icelandic Christmas.

The **Reformation** arrived on **7 November 1550** with the beheading here of **Jón Arason** — the Catholic bishop of *Hólar*, the northern see — and two of his sons. The Lutheran takeover, sealed in blood on this lawn.

A **~magnitude-7 earthquake** (South Iceland Seismic Zone) in **1784** levelled the cathedral; the Danes used it to abolish the bishopric and shift the see to a fishing village called **Reykjavík** — formally, in **1801**. (The last bishop to live at Skálholt, **Hannes Finnsson**, died here in **1796**; the lights went out slowly.) The current church is a **1963 reconstruction** — where the blues-rock band **Kaleo** later recorded a track live, because Iceland.
Its first bishop, from **1056**, was **Ísleifur Gissurarson** — whose son ran the school up at **Haukadalur**.

The district around it is **Biskupstungur**, **the bishop's tongues** — the wedge of land between the **Hvítá** and the **Tungufljót**. A **tunga** is a tongue of land between two rivers, and the bishop in the name is the one on that hill.

The church came before the bishop. **Gissur hvíti** — Ísleifur's own father — is said to have raised the **first church at Skálholt** after the conversion at the **Alþingi in the year 1000**, and **Ísleifur Gissurarson was consecrated the first bishop of Iceland in 1056** and took his seat there. Minjastofnun's phrase for the place is the **head place of Iceland for about 700 years**, and the bishopric ran **continuously from 1056 to 1801**, moving to **Reykjavík** only in the wake of the great natural disasters at the end of the eighteenth century.
The school ran from **Ísleifur's time until 1785**, with short interruptions. Seven centuries of teaching, on a farm.

The 1550 beheading has names and a run-up. **Jón Arason** was executed here on **7 November 1550** together with his sons **Ari** and **the Reverend Björn** — and two years earlier, in **1548**, the Skálholt men had thrown up a **fort east of the churchyard** to hold off his attack, the remains of which are still identifiable on the ground. In **1912** an Englishwoman, **Disney Leith**, paid for a **monument** to him at what is taken to be the execution spot.

The site carries **ten protected archaeological monuments** and **well over a hundred** further age-protected remains. The cathedral standing there now was designed by the state architect **Hörður Bjarnason** and consecrated in **1963** — and Skálholt got a bishop back, a **vígslubiskup**, in **1992.** (Seven hundred years as the centre of the country, ended by an earthquake rather than by politics.)
say: the farm that was Iceland's capital, university and cathedral for 700 years
Iceland's only saint, whose feast on 23 December still anchors the Icelandic Christmas
the last Catholic bishop, beheaded here on 7 November 1550 with two of his sons
"the bishop's tongues", the wedge of land between the Hvítá and the Tungufljót
the state architect of the cathedral standing there now, consecrated 1963

block.title: 🎵 Grímsnes & Kerið
block.sub: Red Walls, Blue Lake, Opera on the Water
block.cue: At Kerið crater.
block.hook: A red crater with a blue lake in the bottom — and in 1987 a county sports club that had just lost a fortune put **opera singers in boats on that lake** and pulled **seven thousand people** in to bail them out.
block.point: A rusting crater, a lake with no inlet, a formation nobody agrees on — and the one time it made the news, it was rescuing a sports club with opera.
block.mic: Seven thousand people sat on the inside of a volcano to watch a man sing arias from a boat. Iceland does not do small fundraisers.
block.weather: Weather pivot: "The red actually goes deeper in the rain, so a grey day makes the crater easier to read, not harder."
bullets: **Kerið is about 6,500 years old** — that is the figure in its own geological description, and a scientific outreach article puts it at about 6,600. **You may have heard me say five to six thousand. That was wrong and I have stopped saying it.**

It is **about 270 m long, 170 m wide and 55 m deep** — deep enough to swallow a seventeen-storey building. The lake in the bottom is **groundwater, 7 to 14 metres deep**, rising and falling with the water table rather than being fed by any stream. It looks turquoise because water absorbs red light first and the floor is dark. And there is life in it: a **2014 paper found ten zooplankton taxa**, mostly rotifers.

**The walls are red because the iron in the scoria has oxidised** — it is rusting, and it is young enough to still be doing it. Give it a few thousand more years and it will blacken like its neighbours. (I used to name the mineral. **Nobody has actually published a mineral analysis of this crater**, so I have stopped doing that too.)

**How it formed is genuinely argued over, and I am not going to pretend otherwise.** Kerið's own geological account says a **scoria cone that collapsed when the magma drained away beneath it** — explicitly not an explosion. A **2024** scientific article says it is probably a **maar**, blown out where magma met groundwater. **Two respectable accounts, opposite mechanisms, same hole in the ground.**

It is the **northernmost crater of the Tjarnarhólar row**, and the **Grímsnes lavas came from twelve separate eruptive centres** covering about **54 km²**. No single big bang — built up in instalments, the way Iceland does most things.

**It is privately owned, and that matters for the ticket.** It has charged a small admission **since June 2013**, which is unusual in a country where walking into a landscape is normally free — the money goes on the path and the stairway down the north wall. The owner is **Kerfélagið ehf.** — a company, not, as I used to say, an association of local farmers: **Arctic Adventures bought all the shares in 2023.**

**And now the concert, because the version on the internet is wrong.** On **Sunday 16 August 1987 at three in the afternoon**, Kerið hosted what Morgunblaðið called ***fyrstu tónleikar í eldgíg á Íslandi*** — **the first concert ever held in a volcanic crater in this country.** The musicians performed **from boats out on the lake**; DV's headline the next day was ***"Fljótandi tónleikar"*** — floating concerts.

**The bill, as the paper printed it two days before:** the opera singer **Kristján Jóhannsson** with **Lára Rafnsdóttir**; **Kristinn Sigmundsson** with **Jónas Ingimundarson**; **Bubbi Morthens**; **Björgvin Halldórsson**; **Magnús Kjartansson's band** with **Erna Gunnarsdóttir**; and **Ásgeir Steingrímsson** on trumpet. **Every one of them played for nothing.** Tickets were **500 krónur**, free for under-fourteens and pensioners.
**Björk was not there.** I told that story for a long time and it is not in a single contemporary report. The rock name on that bill was **Bubbi**.

**Why they did it is the good bit.** **Héraðssambandið Skarphéðinn**, the district sports association, had just lost a fortune on an outdoor festival at **Þjórsárdalur** over the August bank holiday. **Árni Johnsen**, then a member of parliament, got this up to dig them out of it — and **about seven thousand people came.** DV reported the turnout beat the most optimistic hopes in the association and **the debt was paid off.**

One detail from Tíminn that tells you exactly what it was like: **the sound took so long to climb the slope, and the applause so long to come back down, that when the crowd tried to clap along with the singers it threw everybody out.**
say: "the Tub"; the red crater with the blue lake, about 6,500 years old
the volcanic field it sits in; twelve eruptive centres, about 54 km²
the crater row Kerið stands at the north end of
the company that owns it; Arctic Adventures bought the shares in 2023
the opera singer who topped the 1987 bill
the rock name actually on that bill, not the one you have heard
the sports association the concert bailed out
the MP who put it together

block.title: ⚡ Sog River
block.cue: Crossing the Sog.
block.hook: A river only **20 km long** — and for a generation it carried **half of Iceland's electricity**.
block.point: Three small stations on one short river kept a whole country running for half a century — and cost it the biggest trout stock in its biggest lake.
block.mic: Big rivers get the postcards. The Sog quietly ran the lights, and quietly sent the bill.
block.weather: Weather pivot: "Spring-fed, so it looks exactly the same today as it did in the sunshine last week."
bullets: The **Sog** is the **only river draining Þingvallavatn**, Iceland's biggest natural lake, and it runs south to join the **Hvítá** and become the **Ölfusá**.
Short, but enormous in volume — **Iceland's largest spring-fed river**, averaging about **100 m³/s** of lake-clear, gravel-filtered water.

That single outlet is the whole reason the engineers loved it. Þingvallavatn behaves like an **enormous header tank**: it refuses to flood and it refuses to dry, which makes the Sog **one of the steadiest rivers in the country** — exactly what a turbine wants.

Three stations sit on it, and they were built a generation apart. **Ljósafossstöð** (1937), **Írafossstöð** (1953) and **Steingrímsstöð** (1959) — together about **88 MW**, which ran roughly **half of Iceland's electricity** through the 1960s and 70s, until the big highland plants on the **Þjórsá** took over.

**Ljósafoss** opened in **1937** with **two machines of 4.4 MW**; a **third of 5.8 MW** followed in **1944**, taking it to **14.6 MW** — about **105 GWh** a year. Scale was never the point. **Being first was.**

**Írafoss** came online on **16 October 1953** with **two machines of 15.5 MW**. The **third, 16.8 MW, was not added until 1963** — so the famous "48 megawatts" is a *1963* number, not a 1953 one. It harnesses two waterfalls, **Írafoss and Kistufoss**.
**Steingrímsstöð** started up on **6 August 1959**, **26 MW**, and it is the one that dams the **outflow of Þingvallavatn itself**.

And the consequence was entirely domestic. **Ljósafoss quadrupled the electricity available to the capital region**, and **Reykjavík households swapped their coal ranges for electric cookers.** A whole city stopped smelling of smoke because of a drop in a river almost none of them had ever visited.

Where did Iceland's electric age actually start? Not here — in a **carpenter's workshop in Hafnarfjörður**. On **12 December 1904**, **Jóhannes Reykdal** ran a **9 kW** generator off the stream behind his joinery and lit **15 houses — the school and the Good Templars' hall among them — plus the workshop and four street lamps**, in time for Christmas. From one carpenter's stream to all of this, inside a single lifetime.

**The bill came due in the lake.** Damming **Efra-Sog** in 1959 diverted the water past its own channel and into Steingrímsstöð's tunnels, and the flood thrown up by the construction **swept the spawning gravel out of the Útfall**. The Efra-Sog stock had been **the largest brown-trout population in Þingvallavatn**; as a distinct spawning run, it **disappeared**. The lights went on and a fish went out — and that trade is the honest version of this river's story.

the first of its three stations, 1937, 14.6 MW
the middle station, 1953, and the biggest of the three
the last of the three, 1959, 26 MW
the upper reach that was dammed, and the trout stock that went with it
the glacial river the Sog joins
the big drain river the two of them become
Iceland's longest river, whose highland plants took over from the Sog

the town where Iceland's first public electricity lit up in December 1904

block.title: 🌊 Ölfusá
block.cue: Look right at 1–2 o'clock — Ölfusá.
block.hook: Four rivers walk into a valley. Only one of them comes out with a name — and it is carrying more water than anything else in the country.
block.point: Every drop of water that fell on the Golden Circle today — glacier, geyser, waterfall, lake — is squeezing through this one channel.
block.mic: Iceland's biggest river spends most of its journey under other people's names and only gets the credit for the last stretch. Which, frankly, is how most job titles work.
block.weather: Weather pivot: "Rain makes it bigger. Everything I am about to tell you about this river is more true today than it was yesterday."
bullets: **Ölfusá is Iceland's biggest river by volume.** Orkustofnun's long-run measurements put it at about **400 m³ every second** at Selfoss, averaged over **44 years** — against **363 m³/s** for Þjórsá at Urriðafoss, the runner-up. It is emphatically not the longest. It is simply the one nobody could get across.

It is **four systems wearing one name.** The glacial **Hvítá** runs south from **Langjökull** past **Gullfoss**, gathering **Tungufljót** and **Brúará** on the way. The spring-fed **Sog** drains **Þingvallavatn** — Iceland's largest natural lake — down through **Álftavatn**. The two trunk rivers meet under the **eastern flank of Ingólfsfjall**, just above Selfoss, and from there they run as one.

**Veðurstofa Íslands** gauges **5,678 km²** of catchment above its measuring station at Selfoss. Grey glacier-melt and clear spring water, welded into a single channel, with the entire Golden Circle sitting upstream of it.

The channel **zig-zags along the South Iceland Seismic Zone**, following fault lines rather than gravity. Beside it lies **Þjórsárhraunið mikla**, the Great Þjórsá Lava — erupted **about 8,700 years ago** from a fissure **20 to 30 km long** in the **Veiðivötn swarm of the Bárðarbunga system**, it ran **about 130 km to the sea**, **25 cubic kilometres** of it, reaching the coast between the Þjórsá and the Ölfusá. Vísindavefur (Haraldur Sigurðsson, January 2025) calls it *"stærsta hraun sem runnið hefur á jörðinni síðan ísöldinni lauk"* — the largest lava flow that has run anywhere on Earth since the Ice Age ended.

Keep one distinction straight: **largest by volume is not the same as most powerful.** That trophy goes to **Eldgjá**. The same volcanic system also produced **Vatnaöldur in 871** and **Veiðivötn in 1477**. (The biggest thing this island ever erupted is shaped like a field. You cannot see it. That is exactly how big it is.)
say: Iceland's biggest river by volume, about 400 m³ a second
the glacial trunk river, south from Langjökull past Gullfoss
the spring-fed trunk river, draining Þingvallavatn
"Tongue-River", gathered by the Hvítá on the way down
"Bridge-River", the other one the Hvítá gathers
the glacier the Hvítá starts from
the lake the Sog runs out through
the Great Þjórsá Lava beside the river, the largest lava flow on Earth since the Ice Age

block.title: 🏗️ Selfoss
block.cue: Look left, across the river — Selfoss and the Ölfusárbrú.
block.hook: What is more dangerous to a bridge than a world war? Two milk lorries, one tow-rope, and two o'clock in the morning.
block.point: The thing that finally beat this crossing was not an invading army. It was two milk lorries, a tow-rope, and a cable that had been quietly rusting since Queen Victoria.
block.mic: A world war could not take this bridge down. The dairy run managed it at two in the morning.
block.weather: Weather pivot: "You do not need to see anything for this one. Just listen to what is under the wheels."
bullets: **The town exists because of the bridge.** **Ölfusárbrú** was consecrated on **Tuesday 8 September 1891**, and Vegagerðin's own history records it as **the first suspension bridge built in Iceland** — the first of six of that type raised here between 1891 and 1905. The municipality calls it *"þá mesta mannvirki sem Íslendingar höfðu ráðist í"*, the greatest engineering work Icelanders had ever undertaken. Trade collected at the bridgehead and **Selfoss grew up around it.** The old construction hut, **Tryggvaskáli**, is still the oldest building in town.

**The 1891 numbers.** The Alþingi found **60,000 krónur** — 40,000 as a straight grant, 20,000 as a loan to the counties of Árnes and Rangárvellir, repayable over **45 years**. **Tryggvi Gunnarsson** took the contract because nobody else would do it for that money, and Þjóðólfur reported he lost on the job. The bridge was **built in England** and shipped over ready-made, hung from **three twisted iron cables a side**, painted red, and rated to carry **144,000 pounds**.

**Opening day went beautifully right up until they shut it.** Ísafold counted **a full 1,700** people on the riverbank — the largest crowd ever gathered in one place in Iceland outside the capital — and Þjóðólfur reckoned nearer **1,800**, with **just over 1,500** counted walking across in procession behind a brass band. From **just after 11 a.m.** nobody was allowed onto the bridge at all, so the **Governor of Iceland and his entire party had to be rowed across the river** — to attend the opening of the bridge.

**Then at about two in the morning on Wednesday 6 September 1944, the northern main cable snapped.** Two lorries were on the span: a big Dodge carrying **empty milk churns**, towing a second truck that had broken down on the Reykjavík run — both owned by **Kaupfélag Árnesinga**, both on milk haulage for **Mjólkurbú Flóamanna**, the dairy that had been running since December 1929. Both lorries went into the river. **Both drivers lived**; one went under with his truck and surfaced downstream. And get this bit right, because everybody gets it wrong: **the bridge did not fall.** It slumped onto the one surviving cable and hung there, and they used it as a guarded footbridge for another fifteen months.

**It had been warned about, repeatedly.** An engineering inspection that spring produced a **6-tonne limit imposed on 11 May 1944**, repeated on the radio from **29 July**, with bus passengers ordered to get out and walk across. The road director, **Geir Zoëga**, stood on the bank the following afternoon and said only: *"Jæja þá, þá er hún komin svona"* — well then, so that is how it ends. The bridge was **two days short of its 53rd birthday.**

**The replacement opened at midday on Friday 21 December 1945, with no ceremony whatsoever.** A suspension bridge with an **84 m main span** plus a 50 m steel-girder approach on the south bank — **134 m in total**, a **6 m carriageway** and a metre of footway each side, the largest bridge in the country at the time. The steel had been trapped behind wartime export bans in America. By the time it opened, the war it was ordered in the middle of had been over for three months.

**The river still rearranges the town.** On **29 May 2008 at 15:45** the ground let go **twice inside about three seconds** — **Mw 5.8** beneath **Ingólfsfjall**, five kilometres north-west of here, and then **Mw 5.9** on the **Kross fault** five kilometres further west again. Veðurstofa announced **6.3** that afternoon, which is the teleseismic figure; the ground-deformation work settles the pair at a composite **Mw 6.1**. Veðurstofa's GPS station at Selfoss **moved about 20 cm to the south-east and rose 5 cm — permanently.** They **closed the bridges over the Ölfusá** as a precaution, which this river has form for. Twenty-eight people were hurt across Árnessýsla; **nobody was killed.** The town shrugged and carried on growing: **11,000 people on 1 January 2026**, up from **9,812** just two years earlier.

**Bridge number three is going up right now.** First sod cut **20 November 2024** — a **cable-stayed** bridge, **330 m long and 19 m wide**, contractor **ÞG Verk**, about **17.9 billion krónur** for the whole scheme, due **autumn 2028**, and reported on schedule as of **March 2026**.
say: the town that grew up around the crossing; no bridge, no Selfoss
Iceland's first suspension bridge, 1891; today's span is the 1945 replacement
the man who took the contract nobody else wanted
his construction hut, still the oldest building in Selfoss
the dairy whose milk run brought the bridge down
the co-op that owned both lorries
the road director who watched it happen

block.title: 🧭 Ingólfur Arnarson
block.cue: Look right at 3 o'clock — Ingólfsfjall, the flat-topped mountain named after him.
block.hook: Would you move your whole family to an empty island based on where two bits of furniture washed up?
block.point: A saga says he wintered under that mountain. Everything about him being buried inside it was added later, by people who preferred the better story.
block.mic: He chased two pillars across an ocean. We have spent a thousand years chasing his grave up a mountain, and both searches have roughly the same success rate.
block.weather: Weather pivot: "If the mountain has gone, take my word for it — big, flat-topped, and behind us now."
bullets: That flat-topped mountain is **Ingólfsfjall**, **551 m**, and geologically it is a **móbergsstapi** — a table mountain, built under the ice sheet in the middle of the Ice Age. Hyaloclastite with lava layers running through it, capped by a lava shield from the point where the volcano finally broke out above the meltwater. Its high point is the mound called **Inghóll**.

Per the saga, **Ingólfur Arnarson** threw his carved **high-seat pillars** overboard and swore to settle wherever they washed ashore. His slaves **Vífill and Karli** found them in a bay steaming with hot springs, and he named it **Reykjavík**, "Bay of Smokes."

**Here is the bit almost everybody gets wrong.** **Landnámabók does not say Ingólfur is buried on that mountain.** The Sturlubók text says only that he spent his **third winter *"undir Ingólfsfelli fyrir vestan Ölfusá"*** — under Ingólfsfell, west of the Ölfusá — before going on to Reykjavík. The burial in Inghóll is **munnmæli**, oral tradition, and the municipality of Ölfus labels it as exactly that on its own page. A 1964 article in **Goðasteinn** called it **þjóðtrú** and said out loud that it doubted it.

The folklore is better than the history anyway. The mound is said to **open for one night every summer**, and on that night you can reach the treasure buried with him. Nobody has produced the treasure. Nobody has produced the grave either.

**He was not first here, either.** Irish monks — the **Papar** — were already in Iceland and left when the pagans arrived, and a Norseman called **Náttfari** had stayed behind years before. Ingólfur's real title is narrower: **first permanent Norse settler in the saga tradition.** He got the trophy because his descendants ended up running the parliament and writing the record.
We are on **Leið 1**, the Ring Road, only completed in **1974** for the 1,100-year settlement anniversary. Before that, reaching **Höfn** meant hundreds of extra kilometres on rough tracks.

the 551 m table mountain named after him
the mound on top, where tradition, not Landnáma, puts his grave

block.title: 🌋 Hveragerði
block.cue: Look right at 3 o'clock — Hveragerði.
block.hook: A town of **3,342 people** where the ground occasionally rearranges itself — and the locals responded by **building an exhibition around the crack in their floor**.
block.point: Pizza baked by a volcano. Beer brewed with geothermal heat. A shopping centre built over an earthquake crack. All in the same town, all within one postcode.
block.mic: Most towns hide their disasters. Hveragerði put theirs in the lobby and charged admission — except for the crack itself, which is free.
block.weather: Weather pivot: "Cannot see the town? Look for the steam instead. The town is wherever the ground is smoking."
bullets: Hveragerði sits on its own **high-temperature geothermal field**, at the **eastern margin of the Western Volcanic Zone** and the **western end of the South Iceland Seismic Zone**, with the **Hengill** system away to the north-east. Translation: it is steaming and it is on a fault. Fumaroles and mud pots vent **between the houses**.

**On 29 May 2008 the ground let go twice inside about three seconds.** **Mw 5.8** beneath **Ingólfsfjall**, then **Mw 5.9** on the **Kross fault** five kilometres further west — a doublet. Veðurstofa announced **6.3** that afternoon in Icelandic and **6.1** in its English release, and both are right: **6.3 is the teleseismic estimate, 6.1 is what the ground deformation adds up to.** Hveragerði's GPS station moved **199 ± 4 mm to the north-west**, and kept creeping about **30 mm more** until that August. A University of Iceland study found the damage here **averaged 5% of insured value** and was dominated by **non-structural damage and contents rather than collapse** — which is why the town is still standing and still full.

**Rather than hide it, they built an exhibition on it.** **Skjálftinn 2008** — "The Quake" — sits inside the **Sunnumörk** shopping centre, over a fissure that runs through the building. And the best part was never meant to be an exhibit: when the centre was under construction in **2003**, an **earthquake fissure was found in the ground beneath it**, and instead of filling it in they **lit it and left it on show.** Stand on the crack. **Admission is free** — you pay only if you want a turn in the simulator, which runs at over 6.

**The town has a birthday, and it is younger than your grandmother.** It began in **1929** on land of the farm **Vorsabær** in Ölfus: that summer the milk station went up at **Breiðumörk 26**, and the first two houses appeared — **Varmahlíð**, and a summer house at **Fagrihvammur** where **ylrækt**, growing under glass on geothermal heat, started here. A milk station, two dwellings and a greenhouse. That is the entire origin.

**Commercial horticulture began the same year, 1929**, associated with **Sigurður Sigurðsson**; a **45 m² greenhouse went up at Fagrihvammur in 1930** for cucumbers and tomatoes. The **Garðyrkjuskóli ríkisins** at **Reykir** — the state horticultural college — turned out **its first qualified horticulturists in the spring of 1941**, and most of them walked straight out and built nurseries of their own here. The count tells it better than any adjective: **seven horticultural stations in Hveragerði by 1940, twenty by 1950.** Flowers took over in the forties and the place became **blómabærinn**, the flower town.

**And yes, the bananas.** The horticultural college grew them **as an experiment**, never commercially, and the "Europe's largest banana plantation" line you may have read is a myth with excellent legs. Iceland is not, and never was, a banana republic.

For scale: **about 140 people at the end of 1941**, **about 400 by 1946** — the year the district was formally constituted — and **3,342 on 1 January 2026** (Hagstofa Íslands). The **name** is far older than the town: **Hveragerði first appears in Fitjaannáll shortly before 1700**, in an account of an erupting hot spring that **shifted position during earthquakes in 1597**, and by the description of Ölfus written in **1703** the springs were already in daily use for **bathing, boiling and washing**.

Uphill behind the town is **Reykjadalur**, registered by **Náttúrufræðistofnun** as a **high-temperature geothermal area** and described by **Umhverfisstofnun** as a landscape of hot springs, pools, dykes, faults and landslides. It is the valley people walk up to sit in a warm river. Note the two are different places: the **geothermal park is in town**, Reykjadalur is the walk.
And there is a song for this town. **SVVN**, the Icelandic producer who names his tracks after the places on this drive, has one called **Hveragerði** — so this is exactly where it goes on.

block.cue: Through Borgarnes — my own playlist from here to BSÍ.
block.hook: Sixteen tracks, sequenced for exactly this road: quiet while you are tired, warm as the light changes, loud by the time the city shows up.
block.point: Sixteen tracks that go quiet, then loud, in exactly the shape of a good day ending.
block.mic: Right — that is me done talking. My own playlist from here into town: sixteen tracks, all Icelandic, all picked for this exact stretch of road.
bullets: **ACT I — Silence.** You have been awake since six and the whole day is in your bones. Piano, strings, glass-cool modern classical, and a lullaby to close it. That lullaby, track three, is — heads up — technically about infanticide. We will not dwell.

**01 · Sofðu unga ástin mín** — *Hafdís Huld*. Heads up — Iceland's most beloved lullaby is, technically, *about infanticide*. The lyric is from Jóhann Sigurjónsson's 1911 play *Fjalla-Eyvindur*: outlaw's wife Halla sings it to her own baby seconds before throwing the child into a waterfall so she and her fugitive husband can keep running across the highlands. Icelandic parents have nonetheless been singing this to their toddlers ever since. Hafdís Huld cut this version on *Vögguvísur* (2012) at home — while pregnant with her own daughter Arabella. Sleep tight, kids.  [Lullaby thread]

**02 · Flight from the City** — *Jóhann Jóhannsson*. Opening track of *Orphée* (2016) — Jóhann's first solo album for Deutsche Grammophon, and the last solo album he ever made before he died in Berlin in February 2018. The whole record traces the Orpheus myth — death, rebirth, looking back — and was tied directly to his own move from Copenhagen to Berlin. *Flight from the City* is the literal opening of that journey out. Listen to it knowing he never made another.

**03 · Bambaló (feat. Steiney Sigurðardóttir)** — *Gabríel Ólafs*. Plot twist — that “traditional Icelandic lullaby” is actually an *Irish* folk tune that hitchhiked north centuries ago. The word *bambaló* is essentially Icelandic for “rock-a-bye.” Gabríel cut this version with cellist Steiney Sigurðardóttir for *Lullabies for Piano and Cello*. Iceland: still wearing imported clothes, still pulling it off.  [Lullaby thread]

**ACT II — Eyes Open.** The warmth creeps in. Laufey waltzes. **Elín Hall** sings about her dad running *toward* the lava — not a metaphor, in a country built on the stuff. **Ásgeir's** actual father writes his son a song called *The Journey Home*, and the bus suddenly knows where it is going. Then BRÍET, Friðrik Dór and Jón Jónsson, and Valdimar lift it up off the floor.

**04 · Bewitched** — *Laufey*. Title track of the 2023 album that won Laufey the Grammy for Best Traditional Pop Vocal Album in 2024. She wrote it as a “guitar voice waltz” about the moment of falling helplessly into new love after a perfect first date — then asked the **Philharmonia Orchestra** to score the inside of her head. She calls it the song that “sets the sound of the album.” One song. One orchestra. One Grammy. Done.

**05 · Twice** — *Little Dragon*. The piano line you're hearing wasn't supposed to be a Little Dragon song. It was written for a *children's collage book*. Yukimi Nagano walked into the studio, heard drummer Erik Bodin's friend's kids'-book melody, and started scribbling lyrics on the spot. It became Little Dragon's debut single (2007) and got them signed to Peacefrog. Robert Glasper Experiment later covered it. Bedtime story to indie classic, in one studio drop-by.

**06 · Pretty Face** — *Sóley*. Track 2 of Sóley's 2011 debut *We Sink*. The lyric obsesses over the narrator's own reflection in someone else's eyes — validation, identity, choosing to disappear into a dream rather than stay. Listen for the eerie under-hum; that's the song quietly unraveling around you.

**07 · Tachylite** — *Elín Hall*. *Tachylite* is volcanic glass — basaltic lava that cooled too fast to crystallise. Elín Hall calls it “failed lava.” The song is a quiet tribute to her father — an **Icelandic geophysicist who works as a first responder during eruptions**. He runs *toward* the lava. She wrote a song called Failed Lava about him. Released January 2026.

**08 · Heimförin** — *Ásgeir*. *The Journey Home.* The lyrics are by **Ásgeir's dad** — Einar Georg Einarsson, a poet from the village of Laugarbakki — and most of the original Icelandic words on the 2012 debut *Dýrð í dauðaþögn* are his father's. A song called The Journey Home, written by Dad, set to music and sung by son. The album went on to become the best-selling Icelandic debut *of all time*. Family business.  [Family wrote it · Homecoming]

**ACT III — Bags Packed.** Reykjavík widens ahead and the volume comes up. Of Monsters and Men, then **Una Stef** singing *Like Home* — her father wrote track 39 of the other playlist. Agent Fresco blow the doors off. Reykjavík's own mystery woman finally gets a name, seventy years late. Quarashi, and then **Ingó Veðurguð** has the last word.

**09 · In Too Deep** — *BRÍET*. Bríet's debut single — self-released in 2018 when she was eighteen. She set out to write a happy love song and changed direction mid-write; the girl in the song starts smiling and ends pulled under. The track that introduced her voice internationally.

**10 · Á Sama Tíma, Á Sama Stað** — *Friðrik Dór & Jón Jónsson*. The brothers Jónsson. (Yes — actual brothers.) The song was the official 2018 *Þjóðhátíðarlag* — the festival anthem of Þjóðhátíð on the Westman Islands, where every August Iceland packs into a lava-walled valley called Herjólfsdalur and sings whatever song the year's commissioned writer hands them. 2018: the brothers' turn. The country's biggest weekend, scored by two siblings sharing a mic.

**11 · Á Flug** — *Valdimar*. *In Flight.* Valdimar are from **Keflavík** — i.e. the literal airport town this coach just left. From their 2010 debut *Undraland*, released on Geimsteinn, the Keflavík label founded by Rúnar Júlíusson. A song about flight, made by guys you flew over.  [Homecoming]

**12 · Tuna in a Can** — *Of Monsters and Men*. Yes — the song is actually about **canned tuna**. The image — *tuna in a can, sticky from the brine / I thought I'd gone bad, you thought I was fine* — is reportedly Nanna's nod to her **mum's tuna salad**. It became the visual anchor of the entire 2025 album *All Is Love and Pain in the Mouse Parade*; the cover is built around it as “a quilt of familial stories.” Best self-portrait-as-expired-canned-fish in modern indie pop.

**13 · Coming Home** — *Sjonni's Friends*. Sjonni Brink wrote the music. **His wife Þórunn Erna Clausen wrote the lyrics.** So in effect, this is her words sung back to her. He was due to perform it in Iceland's Eurovision semi-final on 29 January 2011 — and died of a brain aneurysm on **17 January 2011, age 36**. Twelve days before the show. Six of his musician friends formed *Vinir Sjonna* / Sjonni's Friends to perform it in his place at Eurovision in Düsseldorf, finishing 20th with 61 points. The song's message — *never know when your time's up, so live and love hard* — was written before he died. Then performed after.  [Family wrote it · Homecoming]

**14 · Howls** — *Agent Fresco*. Track 6 of *Destrier* (2015) — the concept album frontman Arnór Dan Arnarson wrote after **two men attacked him late one night and left him with a broken eye socket and concussion**. The whole record is grief and adrenaline. *Howls* sits at the nostalgic end — *howls of youth, when life would run with lawless legs to race the sun* — the memory of pre-violence freedom the rest of the album is trying to claw back. (A *destrier* is the medieval warhorse bred for battle.)

**15 · Fröken Reykjavík** — *Ríó Tríó / Stórsveit Reykjavíkur*. Music by **Jón Múli Árnason**, lyrics by his brother **Jónas** — the Árnason brothers wrote dozens of Iceland's most-loved mid-century standards together. For seventy-odd years nobody knew who the red-shoed woman walking down Austurstræti actually *was*. Mystery solved in 2023 — director Björn Brynjúlfur Björnsson revealed in *Vísir* that she was his mother, **Jóna Sigurjónsdóttir**. Reykjavík kept its secret for seven decades. Then it broke.  [Family wrote it]

**16 · Jungle Drum** — *Emilíana Torrini*. Co-written with producer Dan Carey, released as a single in March 2009. The “ay-ay-ay” scat hook took it to **No. 1 in Germany, Austria and Belgium** — Torrini's biggest chart hit by a country mile — *after* it got used in the *Germany's Next Topmodel* finale. German rockabilly band The Baseballs covered it the same year. The whole lyric is a heartbeat-as-tribal-drum metaphor. Sometimes a giant pop hit really is just *ay-ay-ay*.

**17 · Mr. Jinx** — *Quarashi*. The earworm hook is sampled from a 1973 American soul cut — **New York City's “Sanity”** — laundered through Reykjavík rap. The song itself never blew up on charts (peaked No. 43 on Radio & Records Alternative). But its second life was sync money — scoring trailers and incidental music for *Alias*, *Smallville*, NBA on TNT (2003–2005), and Madden NFL 2003. Their other *Jinx* track “Stick 'Em Up” snagged the *2 Fast 2 Furious* trailer. Iceland's quiet sync goldmine.

**18 · Takk fyrir mig** — *Ingó Veðurguð*. The last word of the day, and it was written for a party that never happened. This was **Þjóðhátíðarlagið 2020** — the official song of Vestmannaeyjar’s Þjóðhátíð, the biggest weekend in the Icelandic calendar. Ingó wrote it (his brother took a hand in part of it), and then the 2020 festival was called off under gathering restrictions. A thank-you sung to a crowd that never got to turn up. It gets its crowd on this bus instead.  [Homecoming]

block.title: 🏢 Hellisheiðarvirkjun
block.cue: Look right at 2 o'clock — Hellisheiði geothermal plant.
block.hook: Those white plumes are **steam, not smoke** — and the same plant that lights the road also **turns its own exhaust into stone**. Underneath you, permanently.
block.point: It makes the power, heats half the capital, and files its own exhaust underground as gravel. It also taught Iceland that you can trigger earthquakes by being tidy.
block.mic: Most power stations bury their emissions in a report. This one buries them in the rock.
block.weather: Weather pivot: "The worse the weather, the better the plume — on a still cold day the steam columns are the most dramatic thing on this road."
bullets: **Hengill** is not a mountain, it is a **volcanic system** — and it sits where **three zones meet**: the **Reykjanes rift**, the **Western Volcanic Zone** and the **South Iceland Seismic Zone**. Water goes down, comes back at **reservoir temperatures of 260–320°C**, and spins turbines.

**303 megawatts of electricity**, and the arithmetic is satisfying: **six high-pressure turbines of 45 MW plus one low-pressure turbine of 33 MW.** They arrived in stages — **two in 2006, one in 2007, two in 2008, two more in 2011** — so the plant you are looking at was assembled over five years, like flat-pack furniture for a country.

Then the quieter half. **200 MW of heat** goes **27 km down insulated pipes** to warm **more than half the capital region**, which is why Reykjavík never smells of coal. Nationally, **about 90% of the energy used to heat Icelandic homes is geothermal** — Orkustofnun's figure for **2020**.

The trick that makes it safe: the geothermal fluid down there is **hot, corrosive and full of dissolved minerals**, and **it never touches your tap.** It gives up its heat through an exchanger to clean water, and goes back underground.

**Carbfix** is the famous bit, and the famous number needs its footnote. In **2012** a pilot dissolved **175 tonnes of CO₂ in 5,000 tonnes of water** and pumped it in at about **500 m and 35°C**. **Matter et al. (2016)** tracked it: **over 95% turned to carbonate rock in under two years.** That result belongs to *that* pilot — **not automatically to every tonne since**, at different depths, temperatures and rock.

Industrial injection is a different animal: it started on **23 June 2014**, putting the plant's own CO₂ **and H₂S** into fractured basalt at roughly **750 m and over 250°C**. By the end of **2017** that had taken down **23,200 tonnes of CO₂ and 11,800 tonnes of H₂S**. *(The line that "both gases mineralise in about two years" mixes two separate studies — do not say it.)*

And the newest chapter is barely a year old. **ON Power opened a second capture station, Steingerður, on 19 June 2025** — about **30,000 tonnes of CO₂ a year**. Over the twelve months to **30 June 2026** Carbfix reported **99.6% of the CO₂ and 100% of the H₂S** entering the capture system being dissolved, and **cumulative mineralisation past 120,000 tonnes of CO₂ and 50,000 of H₂S**. *(Operator figures — impressive, and only one source, so say who said it.)*

Why bother with the sulphur at all? Because **H₂S stinks and is toxic**, and after the plant opened in 2006 the smell started reaching **Reykjavík** on the wrong wind — around **13,000 tonnes a year** by 2011. Iceland wrote an **ambient H₂S limit in 2010, biting in 2014**, and the cleanup followed. The rotten-egg problem is the reason the rock-making began.

Separately from all that: **Climeworks** pulls CO₂ **out of the open air** here — not out of the turbines. **Orca** started on **8 September 2021** at a nominal **4,000 tonnes a year**; **Mammoth** is nominally **36,000**. Hellisheiði supplies the power, Carbfix supplies the basalt.

**And it is not free.** When large-scale reinjection began at **Húsmúli on 1 September 2011** at about **500 kg a second**, the ground answered immediately: **two magnitude-4 earthquakes on 15 October 2011**, around **forty events above ML 2.5**, eight between **3.0 and 4.0** — felt in **Hveragerði**, the biggest felt in **Reykjavík** — and up to **2 cm** of measured surface movement. Pushing water into a fault system moves faults. That is the honest footnote to the clean-energy story.

the process that dissolves the gas and turns it to stone
the capture station opened in June 2025; the name means "stone-made"
the reinjection field whose 2011 start set off the earthquakes
the town down the hill that felt them
the National Energy Authority, source of the 90% figure
