block.title: ⛰️ Kristnitökuhraun
block.cue: Look left at 9 o'clock — Kristnitökuhraun, the Christianity Lava.
block.hook: Can a volcano vote? Around the year 1000 one appeared to try — and a chieftain took it apart with a single question, without raising his voice.
block.point: A whole country's religion settled by one calm geology question — asked about the wrong lava, about an eruption that was not coming.
block.mic: The pagans claimed a volcano was voting. Snorri pointed out that the ballot box was older than the religion.
block.weather: Weather pivot: "Lava in fog is the honest version. This is roughly what the year 1000 looked like from a distance."
bullets: **The lava out the window has three names, and two of them are the same name.** Properly it is **Svínahraunsbruni** — two historical **ʻaʻā** flows out of the **Eldborgir just west of Lambafell**. In daily speech it is called **Svínahraun**, and so is the much older **Leitahraun** underneath it, which it ran straight over. One of those two flows is the one called **Kristnitökuhraun**, the Christianity Lava. Iceland names a thing twice and then argues about it. Entirely on brand.

It ran **around the year 1000** — Vísindavefur allows **possibly 999** — covered roughly **15 km²**, flowed **north-east** across the flats into **Þrengslin**, and **stopped about where the Ring Road runs now.** You are driving along its edge.

**Now the story, with the actual words, because this one gets told wrong everywhere.** Iceland's chieftains were at **Þingvellir**, and the two sides had just formally declared themselves **out of each other's laws** — which, in a country with one legal system and no army, is how a civil war starts.

***Kristni saga*:** *"Þá kom maðr hlaupandi ok sagði, at jarðeldr var upp kominn í Ölfusi ok mundi hann hlaupa á bæ Þórodds goða."* A man came running and said **earth-fire had come up in Ölfus** and would run over the farm of **Þóroddur goði**. The heathens said: *"Eigi er undr í, at goðin reiðist tölum slíkum"* — no wonder the gods are angry at talk like this.

**Then Snorri goði.** *"Um hvat reiddust goðin, þá er hér brann hraunit, er nú stöndum vér á?"* — **"What were the gods angry about when the lava we are now standing on burned?"** And note exactly where he was pointing: **at the ground under his own feet, at Þingvellir.** Not at this field. He was telling the pagans that their own holy assembly ground was made of the same stuff, laid down by the same fire, long before anyone was around to be blamed for it.

**Only after that** did **Hallur of Síða** buy the lawspeaking from **Þorgeir** — *hálfu hundraði silfrs*, half a hundred of silver, in Kristni saga; **three marks of silver** in Njáls saga, so the two sagas do not even agree on the bribe — and Þorgeir lay down under his cloak for a day, a night and a day.

**And here is the punchline geologists added a thousand years later.** Svínahraunsbruni is the best candidate for the lava in that account. But it ran **north-east, into Þrengslin** — nowhere near the farm everybody was panicking about. Vísindavefur puts it plainly: it seems unlikely the flow ever actually threatened Þóroddur's farm. **The most famous omen in Icelandic history was, on the best reading of the map, a false alarm.**
Footnote with the future in it: this same basalt is what **CarbFix** now uses to turn CO₂ into stone. The rock that once "proved" divine anger is filing industrial emissions.

block.title: ⛰️ Rauðhólar
block.cue: Look ahead — Rauðhólar, the red crater hills.
block.hook: A field of perfect little volcanoes, and **not one of them is real**. We dug half of them up for road gravel — and that turned out to be the reason NASA got interested.
block.point: We shovelled a Mars laboratory into a runway, and then used the hole to do the Mars science.
block.mic: Ninety-eight cones on the 1912 map. A handful left. Most of the rest is underneath Reykjavík Airport, holding up aeroplanes.
block.weather: Weather pivot: "The red goes deeper in the rain, so a grey day actually makes the craters easier to pick out, not harder."
bullets: **They are fake volcanoes.** *Gervigígar* — properly, **rootless cones**. No conduit, no magma chamber underneath, no roots at all. The magma did not come up; it came **sideways**, through closed lava tubes just under the surface.

**What actually happened:** lava from the shield crater **Leiti**, in the eastern **Bláfjöll** ridge, ran about **28 km** all the way down to **Elliðaárvogur** — so fluid that in places the flow is only **0.6 to 0.75 m thick.** Where it crossed wet ground, its own base crust held the water off until the weight cracked it. Water-saturated sediment then met molten lava, and the result was not a polite puff of steam but **repeated explosive mixing** — fragmentation, ash fall, ballistic ejecta — punching **back up through the flow.** Frozen mid-explosion in red scoria. The red is iron oxide. It is rust.

**How old? Genuinely disputed, and I am not going to pretend otherwise.** **Náttúrufræðistofnun Íslands** says **5,200 years**. A University of Iceland thesis says **5,316**. **Vísindavefur** says **4,700**. **Reykjavíkurborg** says **4,500** for the same lava down in Elliðaárdalur. Four institutions, four numbers, one lava. Somewhere between four and a half and five and a half thousand years old.

**How many cones?** The only hard count anybody ever made is **von Komorowicz's map of 1912**, which numbers **98 craters** — cone 53 was one of the biggest — plus **hornitos** on the eastern side that **are not there any more.** He thought they were real scoria cones; nobody had worked out the mechanism yet. Today the field covers about **0.8 km²** and only a handful of intact cones survive, round the edges.

**Because we quarried the rest.** Rauðhólar was largely untouched until about **1940**, when the British occupation brought heavier machinery than this country had ever had and a war's appetite for aggregate. Red scoria made excellent road surfacing and you could shovel it **straight onto a lorry bed**. The single biggest job it fed was **building Reykjavík Airport in Vatnsmýri**. Digging ran hardest from **1940 to 1950**, and was still going in **1949** — into Hringbraut — the year the geologist **Sigurður Þórarinsson** stood up at the Natural History Society's 60th anniversary and said out loud that we were destroying it. An aerial photograph from **28 July 1954** shows how much was already gone.

**It was then protected twice.** As a **náttúruvætti — a natural monument — in 1961**, and again as a **fólkvangur in 1974** (*Auglýsing um fólkvang í Rauðhólum* nr. **185/1974**). Every pseudocrater in Iceland now carries special protection under **náttúruverndarlög nr. 60/2013**.

**Now the Mars part, which is real, and which is not the story people tell.** Nobody trained astronauts here. What happened is that when Mars images began arriving from about **1970**, the crater clusters on them looked exactly like these — same shape, same formation conditions, same volcanism. So between **2002 and 2016**, fieldwork here funded by **NASA's Mars Data Analysis Program, Mars Fundamental Research Program and NASA Postdoctoral Program** used the **quarry faces** — the damage — to work out how a rootless cone is built on the inside, and applied it to the Red Planet. **The vandalism is the reason the science was possible.** There is nowhere else in Iceland you can look inside one of these.

For scale, Iceland's big pseudocrater fields are **Landbrotshólar at 150 km²**, **Álftavershólar at 35**, **Mývatn at 30** and **Aðaldalur at 28**. Rauðhólar is **0.8**. It is the small one. It is also the one twenty minutes from a capital city, which is exactly why it went under a runway.
The same lava built **Tröllabörn** west of Lækjarbotnar, and the caves **Raufarhólshellir** and **Árnahellir**.

The shallow lake beside them is **Rauðavatn**, "Red Water", and that scruffy belt of trees is the **oldest deliberate woodland in the Reykjavík area.** In **1901** about eighty shareholders founded **Skógræktarfélag Reykjavíkur**, bought **six hectares** by the lake and put the Danish forester **C. E. Flensborg** in charge of the summers. They dug **8,600 holes in 1902** and planted about **8,000 rowan** the next summer. Frost killed nearly all of it, and the fence never held — a newspaper in **1918** grumbled that the livestock *gengur þar inn og út*, in and out as they pleased. Only after the Second World War, with close to **60,000 plants**, did it finally take. The oldest mountain pines by the lake are now **over a hundred years old.** (How do you find your way out of an Icelandic forest? Stand up. This is where somebody first set out to ruin that joke, and they have been at it for a hundred and twenty-four years.)

**Ari the Wise** wrote in *Íslendingabók* that at settlement Iceland was *viði vaxið milli fjalls og fjöru* — wooded from the mountains to the shore. Today woodland covers about **1.5%** of the country.

Behind the cones lies **Elliðavatn**, and on a low spit in it, **Þingnes**: **16–17 surface ruins, at least 18 structures**, and two nested circles nobody has ever pinned a function on. The state registers it as *hinn forni Kjalarnessþingstaður*, the ancient Kjalarnes assembly place — **signed 25 October 1930, entered 16 November 1938.** Whether it really is the þing **Ari fróði** put on **Kjalarnes**, fourteen kilometres that way, has never been proven by anybody.

And the electricity arc closes here: the **Elliðaár** valley below held **Reykjavík's first power station, opened in 1921** — seventeen years after **Reykdal's carpentry-shop plant** lit the nation's first bulbs in Hafnarfjörður.

block.title: 🏔️ Langjökull
block.cue: Heading up onto Langjökull — Iceland's second-largest ice cap.
block.hook: That waterfall you just photographed at Gullfoss? It's **this glacier crying.** Now we're going to ride snowmobiles across the thing doing the crying — a **580-metre-thick bank of ice, currently in overdraft.**
block.point: You are riding a snowmobile across a **1,400-metre-high freshwater reservoir that sits on two volcanoes and is quietly melting on a deadline.** Nowhere else does "just a bit of snow" carry that much backstory.
block.mic: We put you on a snowmobile on top of the very glacier that feeds every waterfall, geyser pool and fissure you've admired all day. Ride gently — you're on the source code.
block.weather: Weather pivot: "If the ice cap has gone into the cloud, that is normal. It makes its own weather up there."
bullets: **Langjökull** means **"Long Glacier"** — Icelandic place-naming at its most ruthlessly literal, like nicknaming a tall bloke "Tall Man." It's **Iceland's second-largest ice cap** (after Vatnajökull): roughly **870–900 km²**, about **50 km long, up to 20 km wide**, holding on the order of **190 km³ of ice** up to **~580 m thick** and topping out just over **1,400 metres**. You'll be snowmobiling on more frozen water than most countries own.

**Fire directly under the ice:** this isn't just frozen scenery — it's a **lid on two active volcanic systems**, **Prestahnúkur** and **Hveravellir**. The calm white surface you're carving across has a temper it simply hasn't used lately.

**The waterworks of the whole Golden Circle:** Langjökull's meltwater feeds the **Hvítá** — the river that becomes **Gullfoss** — plus the **Ölfusá** system, and, via groundwater filtered through porous lava, the eerily clear **Silfra** fissure back at Þingvellir. Everything wet you've seen today drained off the glacier under your skis.

**The timer:** Langjökull has been **losing mass steadily for decades**, and Institute of Earth Sciences modelling projects it could be **largely gone within about 150 years** on present warming — the fastest-shrinking of Iceland's big caps. Snowmobiling here is less "extreme sport," more "**visiting a patient you'll outlive.**"

For the fully indoors version, the **"Into the Glacier"** ice tunnel — the world's largest man-made bore into a glacier, **~500 m** long, opened **1 June 2015** from the Húsafell side — lets you walk *inside* Langjökull past ice older than the settlement of Iceland. A museum you have to dig.

block.title: ♨️ Gamla Laugin
block.sub: The "Secret" Lagoon That Taught Iceland to Swim
block.cue: At Flúðir — the Secret Lagoon.
block.hook: A "secret" lagoon that's **135 years old** and printed on every Golden Circle coach map. Some secret. It's the **oldest swimming pool in Iceland** — and the spot where the whole country first learned not to drown.
block.point: The oldest pool in the country, the classroom where Iceland learned to swim, and a live geyser for a tap — all in one steaming field off the Golden Circle.
block.mic: Iceland's worst-kept secret: a 135-year-old bath that taught a nation to swim, took a 67-year nap, and woke up still warm.
block.weather: Weather pivot: "You are getting in the water anyway. The forecast stops mattering at the changing rooms."
bullets: **Gamla Laugin** ("the Old Pool") at **Hverahólmi** by Flúðir was **built in 1891** — **Iceland's oldest surviving swimming pool**, older than the national grid, the republic, and your great-grandparents. The "Secret Lagoon" branding was bolted on 120-odd years later; the water never went anywhere.
Before it was a pool it was a **parliament**: the local Flúðir assembly met on this exact patch until **1894**. Iceland's founding instinct, again — find a warm bit of ground and hold a vote on it.

In **1909** it hosted **Iceland's first formal swimming lessons** — **32 men** in the debut course, girls following by **1911** — and taught the district every summer until **1947**. In a country ringed by a lethal North Atlantic, teaching the nation to swim in a hot bath was a genuinely brilliant life-hack.
Then it was **abandoned for nearly 70 years** — the village built a modern pool and left the old one to the algae. Scrubbed up and reborn on **7 June 2014**, history intact.

The water sits at **38–40°C year-round**, sulphur-rich, kept topped up **100% by the surrounding hot springs** — including a **baby geyser, Litli Geysir**, that fires every few minutes just off the deck. The one hot tub on Earth plumbed straight into a working geyser.
say: "the Old Pool", a.k.a. the Secret Lagoon, built 1891
the geothermal spot by Flúðir it sits on
the greenhouse-and-mushroom village beside it, whose assembly met here until 1894
the baby geyser off the deck that fires every few minutes

block.title: 🌊 Ölfusá Intro
block.cue: Look right at 1–2 o'clock — Ölfusá, ahead in the lowlands.
block.hook: The big drain, ahead in the lowlands. It gathers a huge slice of the highlands and ends at villages now best known for **a prison and a lost harbour**.
block.point: From up here it's just a pale line on the flats. Down at Selfoss, it's the biggest river in the country.
block.mic: At the far end of that pale line: two harbours that lost their trade, and one address nobody checks out of early.
block.weather: Weather pivot: "Rain makes it bigger. Everything I am about to tell you about this river is more true today."
bullets: That pale line across the lowlands ahead is the **Ölfusá**. Every drop of water we'll see today ends up in it — but save the numbers, we'll be standing on its bank at Selfoss.
What's worth knowing from up here is what sits at the far end of it — the two villages where it meets the sea, and the prison just inland.
It empties by **Eyrarbakki** and **Stokkseyri** — once among Iceland's busiest harbours, until the deeper port at Þorlákshöfn stole the trade.
Just inland sits **Litla-Hraun**, Iceland's main maximum-security prison.

Iceland's main maximum-security prison, just inland

block.title: 🫧 Öskjuhlíð & Perlan
block.sub: The Lid On The City's Hot Water
block.cue: Look right at 3 o'clock — the wooded hill with the glass dome on top.
block.hook: That dome is a **lid.** Under it sit **six steel tanks**, each **ten metres tall and twenty-three across**, each holding about **four million litres** of water at **eighty degrees** — so Reykjavík can run a bath at seven in the morning.
block.point: A hill they quarried away, occupied, then filled with the city's hot water and put a restaurant on.
block.mic: Every building you will see today is heated by water like that. Iceland does not burn anything to keep warm — it just pumps up what is already hot.
block.weather: Weather pivot: "If the dome has gone in the murk, you are not missing much of a view today either — which is rather the point of the tanks underneath it."
bullets: **Öskjuhlíð** is **61 metres** high and made of **Reykjavíkurgrágrýti** — grey basalt erupted from Mosfellsheiði late in the Ice Age, then scraped smooth by glaciers. About **ten thousand years ago it was an island.** The old shoreline round here sits **42 metres** above today's sea.

From **1913** they blasted the north face out and ran it down to the harbour on a **purpose-built railway** — one of the very few stretches of railway Iceland has ever had. **The stone became the harbour. The hole became the bowling alley.**

The **Allies took this hill in 1940** and built all over it once the airfield went into Vatnsmýri in **1941.** It is now **the best-preserved military ground in Reykjavík** — pillboxes, command bunkers, trenches, blast walls, and the floors of hundreds of Nissen huts still in the trees.

The first hot-water tank went up in **1940**, more followed, two more in **1966**, and the lot was **demolished in 1986 to 87** and rebuilt. **Perlan** went on top — architect **Ingimundur Sveinsson**, opened **21 June 1991.** The steel frame does two jobs: it ties the tanks together and it is the dome.

The wood is deliberate. Planting started **after about 1950** on a council scheme, and the tallest conifers now clear **15 metres** — birch, mountain pine, Sitka spruce, Alaska poplar. In a country with almost no forest, somebody had to decide to put one here.
say: the 61 m basalt hill the tanks stand on
'the pearl', the dome over six hot-water tanks, opened 1991
the grey Ice Age basalt the hill is made of

block.title: 🧺 Þvottalaugarnar
block.sub: Why The Main Shopping Street Is Called Laundry Road
block.cue: Look left — the green valley of Laugardalur opening up.
block.hook: Reykjavík's main shopping street is called **Laugavegur.** Everyone translates it as something romantic. It means **the road out to the washing pools** — and they are in that valley, and this is the road.
block.point: The hot water that ended the washerwomen's walk is the same hot water heating every building you will see today.
block.mic: So when a guidebook tells you Laugavegur is Reykjavík's Oxford Street — it is, but it started as the route to the launderette.
block.weather: Weather pivot: "On a day like this you can see the steam from the valley better than anything else, which is how they found the place to begin with."
bullets: Out there are the **Þvottalaugarnar**, hot springs the town did its laundry in. First written down in **1672** by the physician **Þorkell Arngrímsson Vídalín**, who reckoned the water healed people. **By about 1830 nearly every household in Reykjavík was using them.**

Women carried the washing out, boiled it, beat it, and carried it home wet. The town council finally voted in **1885** to build them a proper road, and it was laid in **1886.** That road is **Laugavegur.** By **1900** it was the most populous street in town with over **700 residents** — a laundry track that turned into the high street.

The name runs the other way from what people assume. The **pool** is the oldest name. **Laugardalur**, **Laugarnes**, **Laugalækur**, **Laugavegur** — all of them are named after the *laug*, not the other way about.

In **1928** they drilled the first borehole beside the pools and got **87 degree** water. In **1930** they ran a **three kilometre pipe** from there to **Austurbæjarskóli** — **Iceland's first municipal district heating.** By **1937** it warmed 58 houses.

**The same year the pipe was switched on, 1930, the laundry stopped.** The springs did not run out. They got promoted. There is a sculpture in the valley, **Þvottakonan** by **Ásmundur Sveinsson**, 1958, for the women who made the walk.
say: 'the valley of the pools', off to the left

block.title: 🏞️ Elliðaárdalur & Paradísardalur
block.cue: Look right at 2 o'clock — Elliðaárdalur.
block.hook: To joggers it's a postcard. To a geologist, it's a **crime scene** — ten thousand years of Iceland trying, and failing, to stay quiet.
block.point: It looks like a Sunday-stroll park. It's a five-thousand-year-old construction site nobody ever closed.
block.mic: A volcano split the river. The Vikings claimed it. The British fortified it. The river is still working overtime to undo all of it.
block.weather: Weather pivot: "The valley looks its best wet. That river is the reason anything in this city is green."
bullets: The whole valley was redesigned when **Leiti** erupted. The crater is **Leitin**, east of **Bláfjöll**, the lava is **Leitahraun**, and it is a textbook **helluhraun** — the smooth, ropy kind you can walk on. It poured down here, hit the river and **split it in two**. Before, one river. After, two.

How long ago? Somebody dug the answer out of this valley: a radiocarbon date on **birch charcoal found underneath the lava, right here in Elliðaárdalur**, gives **about 4,600 years**. Other estimates for the same lava run up to about 5,300 — the same spread of dates that the **Rauðhólar** craters have, and for a very good reason. **Rauðhólar sit in this lava.** Same eruption, different souvenir.
Every waterfall in the valley is the river's four-and-a-half-thousand-year project to saw back down through that basalt to the sea. It is not finished.

The **Elliðaá** is one of very few **capital-city rivers anywhere with a wild Atlantic salmon run** — and there is a camera counter in it, so this is a counted number, not a boast. **1,533 fish in 2009**; **1,067 in 2003**. If you have heard "two and a half thousand salmon", that number is real but it is the wrong animal: **2,500 is a batch of smolts**, not returning adults.

Reykjavík was so taken with the river it **bought the whole thing in 1906**. Your city buys parks. We bought a river. The power station, **Elliðaárstöð, was switched on on 27 June 1921** and is still down there humming.

One kilometre of this valley has hosted a **1750s wool mill**, a **drowning pool at Skötufoss** for women convicted of "moral crimes", outlaws living in the lava tubes, **British WWII Quonset huts**, and a century-old hydro plant. And most Icelandically of all, a **burst pipe in 1998** flooded the place and washed **ten thousand years of buried history back into daylight in a single weekend.** Even the plumbing does archaeology here.

the neighbouring valley named alongside it here
the lava from the crater Leitin, east of Bláfjöll, that split the river
smooth ropy lava, the kind this is

block.title: 🗻 Vífilsfell
block.sub: The Mountain Named After A Slave
block.cue: Look ahead at 1 o'clock — the stepped mountain with the flat shelf.
block.hook: There is a mountain out that window **named after a slave** — and the naming is recorded in Iceland's founding text itself.
block.point: Two eruptions, two ice ages, one mountain — and it is named after a freed slave rather than the man who freed him.
block.mic: Ingólfur got a statue and a hill in the middle of Reykjavík. Vífill got 655 metres of it.
block.weather: Weather pivot: "If the top is in cloud you are still seeing the shelf, and the shelf is the older mountain — so you are getting the first eruption and missing the second."
bullets: **Landnámabók** puts it in seven words: ***"við hann er kennt Vífilsfell"*** — the mountain is named for him. **Vífill** was one of **Ingólfur Arnarson's** two slaves, sent along the coast to hunt for his high-seat pillars. **Ingólfur gave Vífill his freedom.** The other one, **Karli**, said they had crossed good country only to settle an outlying headland, and walked off. **Only Vífill was freed** — and only Vífill got a mountain.
It is **655 metres**, the highest ground in Kópavogur. And that shelf halfway up is the interesting part.

**It is two mountains stacked.** The shelf is a **stapi** — a tuya — móberg built under ice and then capped with lava once the eruption melted through and the meltwater could no longer reach the vent. **The summit above it is a second, younger móberg mountain sitting on top of the first**, from a separate eruption in **probably a different ice age.**

That younger top sits on a **north-west to south-east fissure**, which is odd. Almost every crack in South Iceland runs **north-east to south-west.** This one is at right angles to the grain of the country.
say: 655 m, named for Ingólfur's freed slave Vífill
a tuya, a flat-topped mountain built under ice then capped with lava
the brown rock made when lava erupts under a glacier

block.title: 🌊 Þjórsá
block.cue: Look right at 1–2 o'clock — Þjórsá and its floodplain.
block.hook: Up ahead we cross **Iceland's longest river** — a **230 km** glacial spine that the settlers argued beside and engineers turned into the country's biggest battery.
block.point: Every crossing passes over the main drain — and the biggest battery — for a big chunk of Iceland's backbone.
block.mic: Selfoss had its milk-truck drama. Þjórsá is the **patient heavyweight** — moving a whole highland's worth of water, and a serious slice of the national grid, to the sea.
block.weather: Weather pivot: "Weather barely touches this river. It drains a highland catchment, so it runs much the same in sun or sleet."
bullets: **Þjórsá** runs **230 km** to the sea, **Iceland's longest river**, draining a **7,530 km²** catchment. And it does not start where almost everyone says it does: it begins up in **Þjórsárdrög on northern Sprengisandur**, where the headstream carries the lovely name **Bergvatnskvísl**. The Hofsjökull line you will hear is a muddle — Hofsjökull and Vatnajökull feed the *catchment* that the power stations run on, which is not the same as the river's source.
By the time it reaches **Urriðafoss**, just below the bridge, it is moving about **360 cubic metres a second**. Not a river you paddle absent-mindedly.

**Urriðafoss** is **Iceland's most voluminous waterfall** — *vatnsmesti foss*, the one with the greatest average flow. It is not the tallest and it is not the most powerful; **Dettifoss** up north is the *aflmesti*, the most powerful. The two get swapped so reliably that the University of Iceland has had to correct it in print. Low, wide and unphotogenic beats tall and famous, if the metric is water.

Every winter the river builds an ice jam here with its own name, the **Urriðafosshrönn** — ice and slush packing in until Iceland's most voluminous waterfall is simply not visible, buried under its own river. Landsvirkjun surveyed it in the winter of 2002–03; the numbers are in their report and not in my mouth.

It does more electrical work than any river in Iceland. The classic cascade on the **Þjórsá–Tungnaá** system is **six stations** — Búrfell, Sultartangi, Hrauneyjafoss, Vatnsfell, Sigalda and Búðarháls, the last of those only since **2014**. Landsvirkjun now counts **seven**, because Búrfell got a second station, and the proposed **Hvammur** would be the eighth. The original **Búrfell came online on 16 September 1969**, and the reason a country of 380,000 people generates this much electricity is spelled **aluminium**.

People have wanted **Urriðafoss** itself since **1927**, when the poet **Einar Benediktsson's** company **Titan** was granted permission for a **160,000-horsepower** station here and never turned a sod. The modern version is **Urriðafossvirkjun** — **140 MW**, about **1,037 GWh a year** — and on **17 February 2026** Alþingi left it in **biðflokkur**, the hold category, with the committee specifically recommending against moving it to the use category. A hundred years of wanting, and the river is still winning on points.

Midstream sits the island of **Árnes**, and the district is still called **Árnessýsla** after an assembly nobody can now locate. Alþingi's own research material says the scholars are split: **no assembly booths have ever been identified on the island**, while **thirty to forty** booth-like structures are recorded at **Búði**, on the north bank, where a spring assembly serving **three goðorð** ran until **963**. A whole county named after a meeting, and we have lost the room.

About the name. **Landnámabók** says the settler **Þórarinn Þorkelsson** sailed into the mouth with a **bull's head on his prow**, giving *Þjórsá*, the bull river — **Árnastofnun** records the traditional reading as **Bolafljót**. But **Þórhallur Vilmundarson** argued the original was ***Þjótsá***, from the verb for roaring, pointing at the farm on the bank still called **Þjótandi**, "the one that roars". A river named either for a cow's head or for the noise it makes. Iceland has never settled it.
say: Iceland's longest river, 230 km to the sea
the headwaters on northern Sprengisandur where it actually begins
the midstream island that gave Árnessýsla its name
"trout falls", Iceland's most voluminous waterfall, just below the bridge
the winter ice jam that buries it
"the one that roars", the farm on the bank that may have named the river

block.title: 🕳️ Hella
block.cue: Coming up ahead — the caves of Hella, cut into the bank of the Ytri-Rangá.
block.hook: Long before the Vikings arrived with longships, someone else may already have been here — **literally hiding in the walls**.
block.point: Some of the oldest, strangest archaeology in the country — proof that in Iceland, history isn't just on the surface. Sometimes it's dug into the hillside you're driving past.
block.mic: Most towns keep their history in a museum. Hella keeps a chunk of it in the basement — and isn't sure who moved in first.
block.weather: Weather pivot: "You will not see the caves from here in any weather. They are cut into the bank, which is rather the point of them."
bullets: Carved into the soft sandstone beside the **Ytri-Rangá** is a cluster of **man-made caves**, some with simple **crosses** and **stone benches** cut into the wall.

A popular theory ties them to the **Papar** — the Irish monks that **Íslendingabók** and **Landnámabók** both say were in Iceland *before* the Norse, and who left the moment longships appeared. Tempting. But honestly: the dating is **disputed**, and **no archaeology has confirmed a pre-Norse origin** for these caves. Treat it as suggestive, not settled. The caves are real, the crosses are real, the monks are a maybe.

The town itself is a newcomer by comparison. **Hella dates from 1927**, when a trader who had been working out of **Rauðalækur** bought a small plot out of the land of the farm **Helluvað**, right by the bridge over the Ytri-Rangá, and opened a general store — and a slaughterhouse. Nothing anchors a settlement like being able to buy your groceries and butcher your lamb in one stop.
And the farm's name is the town's name. **Helluvað** gave **Hella** — so a place famous for holes in the rock is named after the flat slab of rock at the ford.
Today it is the pit-stop with **volcanoes on the skyline** (Hekla, up the road), **horses in the fields** — this is **Rangárvellir** horse country — and possibly **monks in the basement**.
say: the town by the bridge, dating from 1927
the farm whose land it was bought out of, and where the name comes from
the river the caves are carved beside
the Irish monks said to have been here before the Norse
the horse-breeding district around the town

block.title: 🐟 Ægissíðufoss
block.sub: The Best Salmon River In Iceland Is Not A Salmon River
block.cue: Look ahead at 12 o'clock — the Ytri-Rangá going over its lower falls.
block.hook: In **2022** this river was **the top-producing salmon fishery in the whole of Iceland** — **5,112 fish.** And before the 1970s it had **essentially no salmon in it at all.**
block.point: A cold, clear, gravel-poor river that had no salmon, engineered into the best salmon fishery in the country.
block.mic: It shares its name with the caves we just passed at Ægissíða — same farm, completely different story. One is a river cutting rock. The other is people cutting sandstone.
block.weather: Weather pivot: "You will hear it before you see it in this. The Rangá never runs low, which is the whole point of a spring river."
bullets: The **Ytri-Rangá** is a **60 km spring-fed river** rising in Rangárbotnar north of Hekla, running at about **50 cubic metres a second** and barely changing — the springs come out at **4 to 6 degrees** all year, so it does not flood in summer and it does not freeze.

**And that is exactly why it had no salmon.** The bed is too fine, the water too cold, and salmon fry could never get a grip. **These were trout rivers.** Then people started releasing smolts by the hundred thousand.

In **1982** they cut a **fish ladder** into this waterfall, and another into Árbæjarfoss upstream in **1985.** Both carry **fish counters**, and the one here is the river's census point. In **2024** it logged **6,400 salmon** going up, from which the river reckoned about **twelve thousand** came in off the sea.
The state fisheries institute is careful enough about it that **when it publishes Iceland's wild salmon figure, it subtracts these rivers first.**
The falls also mark a line in the ground. The old **interglacial shield lavas** that make up all the flat farmland north of here **stop right at Ægissíðufoss.** Everything past it is younger.
say: the lower falls on the Ytri-Rangá, fish ladder cut in 1982
'the outer Rangá', a 60 km spring-fed river
a spring river, fed from the ground rather than off a glacier

block.title: 🏡 Keldur
block.cue: Look left at 10 o'clock — Keldur turf farm.
block.hook: What did a "McMansion" look like for a powerful Icelandic chieftain **800 years ago**? It came with **its own escape tunnel**.
block.point: Not a quaint old farm. **Medieval security architecture** built straight into the hillside.
block.mic: Keldur is basically a Viking-age panic room and getaway car disguised as a cosy turf farm.
block.weather: Weather pivot: "You will not see Keldur today, and nobody ever does from this road. It is eleven kilometres inland — which is exactly why it is still standing."
bullets: **Keldur** is, in *Morgunblaðið*'s exact formulation, **the oldest turf farm in the country — and part of it is the oldest house in the country.** Not the oldest ruin. The oldest house. The National Museum traces the hall to the **late 1100s**, framed while the sagas were still being lived rather than written, and **Bautasteinn** calls it the largest preserved turf farm in the whole south.

It was a seat of the **Oddaverjar**, the clan the sagas call the **"Kings of the South"**, and it stands square in **Njáls saga** country — its first inhabitant, **Ingjaldur Höskuldsson**, is named in the saga itself.
The thick turf walls were not decoration, they were **climate technology**: keeping people, animals and food alive through long wet winters on an island with almost no timber to spare.

And then the good bit. A hidden **underground tunnel** runs from the hall down toward a stream. **Matthías Þórðarson published it in 1932** under the title *Forn jarðgöng fundin á Keldum* — "ancient tunnel found at Keldur" — and archaeologists went back to it again in **1998**. It is not romantic and it is not a secret passage for lovers. It is an **escape route**, in case somebody came in the night to **burn the house down with everyone asleep inside**. In this neighbourhood that was not paranoia. Ask Njáll.

Here is a detail worth the bus's time: the man who dug that tunnel out, **Matthías Þórðarson**, also spent years digging at **Bergþórshvoll**, looking for the burning itself. One archaeologist, two ends of the same story — the fire, and the way out of it.

You cannot see any of this from the road. Keldur sits about **eleven kilometres inland up road 264**, behind a ridge, which is precisely why it survived. It is owned by **Þjóðminjasafn Íslands** and open to visitors from **1 June to 31 August** — and it is still a working farm, with a farmer living on it.
say: the oldest turf farm in Iceland, with its own escape tunnel
the clan the sagas call the Kings of the South, whose seat this was
its first inhabitant, named in Njáls saga
the archaeologist who published the tunnel in 1932, and who also dug Bergþórshvoll
a turf farmhouse, the building type this is the oldest of
the saga hero whose country this farm stands in

block.title: 🏘️ Hvolsvöllur
block.cue: Look ahead at 12 o'clock — Hvolsvöllur.
block.hook: A normal-looking service town that comes with its own **blood-soaked medieval bestseller** — and a field where people have actually dug for the ending.
block.point: Most towns have a petrol station and a supermarket. This one has a community tapestry of **betrayals, burnings and bad legal advice** — and a museum plugged into the next eruption.
block.mic: Welcome to Njáll's neighbourhood — where the local reading list doubles as a murder map.
block.weather: Weather pivot: "If the village is in murk, that is Njáll's country behaving normally. The saga has far more bad weather in it than good."
bullets: **Hvolsvöllur** is the last full-service fuel stop before Vík, planted in the heart of **Brennu-Njáls saga** country — Iceland's **longest, bloodiest, most carefully built** family saga. The farms and low hills around you are its stage.

Written **late in the 1200s** but set around **the year 1000**, its set-piece is the **brenna** — the burning of **Njáll**, his wife **Bergþóra** and their sons at **Bergþórshvoll**, on the flat land just east of here, which the saga's own chronology puts around **1011**. *Game of Thrones*, except half the cast also had to be home for the haymaking.

And here is the part that makes it more than a story. **People went and dug it up.** **Sigurður Vigfússon** excavated Bergþórshvoll in **1883 and 1885**; the national antiquarian **Matthías Þórðarson** went back in **1927**, again in **1931**, and the work ran on to **1951** — seventy years of Icelanders looking for one fire. **They did find a burnt layer**, right at the bottom of the occupation deposits, from buildings that had plainly burned, its edges curled up against the walls. What nobody has ever been able to say is that it was **his** fire.

Odder still: **Bergþórshvoll is not in Landnámabók at all** — it was not a settlement farm. But Landnáma **twice mentions Njáll's burning as something everybody already knew about.** The event outran the address.

In town: the **Saga Centre**, with a **replica Viking hall**, a model of **Þingvellir around the year 1000**, and the long **Njáls saga tapestry**, stitched by locals and visitors — a medieval soap opera in coloured thread, still being sewn.

Next door, the **LAVA Centre** opened in **2017**, and it was put here on purpose: it sits between **four active volcanic systems** — Hekla, Katla, Eyjafjallajökull and the Westman Islands, all inside 50 km — with a live seismograph reading the ground under your feet. A museum wired to the next eruption.
say: the last full-service fuel stop before Vík
the saga hero burned with his family, around 1011 in the saga's own reckoning
"Burnt Njáll", Iceland's longest and bloodiest family saga
Njáll's farm on the flat land just east, dug for the burning three times over seventy years
a saga "burning-in", the set-piece of that story
the village down the coast this is the last fuel stop before

block.title: 🐦 Vestmannaeyjar
block.cue: Look right at 2 o'clock — the Westman Islands out to sea.
block.hook: In **1973** a brand-new volcano opened at the edge of a working fishing town — and the town **fought it with a fire hose and a dredger, and ended up with a better harbour than it started with.**
block.point: One of the very few places on Earth where a town fought a volcano with pumps and pipe — and finished the argument with a better harbour.
block.mic: The volcano tried to close the harbour. The islanders pumped six million tonnes of the North Atlantic at it and said: we will take the upgrade, thanks.
block.weather: Weather pivot: "No islands today? They are further out than they look — but the ferry still only takes half an hour, which tells you how good the boat is."
bullets: **Just before two in the morning on 23 January 1973**, a fissure tore open on the eastern side of **Heimaey**. Icelandic accounts give it as **1,600 metres with 30 to 40 vents**; the **USGS** says it opened to about **two kilometres, right across the island from shore to shore**, with submarine activity at both ends. Out of it came a volcano that had not existed the day before: **Eldfell**, "Fire Mountain", which grew to roughly the height of **Helgafell** standing next to it.
**The town was 5,273 people** — that is the census count of **1 December 1972**, seven weeks earlier. **Nearly all of them were off the island and safely on the mainland within six hours.**

**The reason it worked is that the fishing fleet was in port.** Iceland has **no army**; the evacuation was run by the people who happened to own boats. The explanation everybody gives — **including me** — is that a storm the day before had kept the fleet in. Be straight about it: **the fleet being in port is documented; the storm is the story that goes with it.**

**It did not stop for five and a half months.** The eruption **was not declared over until 3 July 1973.** For the whole of that spring Heimaey was a disaster zone, a building site and an active volcano at the same time, and people went to work in it.

**The damage, counted by early May:** about **300 buildings engulfed by lava or gutted by fire**, and another **60 to 70 homes buried completely by tephra**. Iceland's own Pompeii — and some of those houses have since been **dug back out** and left open at the **Eldheimar** museum.

**Then the part nobody believes.** On **6 February** the **Vestmannaeyjar fire brigade** started spraying seawater at the lava front with hoses — about **100 litres a second**, which against a lava flow is a rounding error. On **1 March** the dredger **Sandey** arrived with **56-centimetre steel pipe** and pushed about **400 litres a second**. American equipment landed on **26 March**. By the time the pumps stopped on **10 July** they had put roughly **eight million cubic yards of North Atlantic seawater** onto the flow, through **43 pumps** and **more than nineteen miles — thirty kilometres — of pipe, three-quarters of it plastic.**

**And it worked.** The tongue of lava that had almost closed the harbour entrance **stopped where they cooled it**, and the USGS is blunt about what happened next: it **is now acting as a breakwater, protecting the harbour from storms.** The volcano tried to shut the port. The port came out **better sheltered than before.**
The lava and tephra also added **nearly a square mile** of new ground — **about 20% more island** than they started with.

**On the deaths, be straight, because it is genuinely contested.** **Icelandic institutional sources record no deaths from the eruption.** **The USGS records one fatality — a man overcome by gas inside a building** — with several others partially affected. Those two accounts have **never been reconciled**, and I am not going to reconcile them for you out of a bus window. What I will say is that **the lurid version some guides tell, a looter overcome in a pharmacy basement, is not documented in any source I would stand behind.** A town of **5,273** got out from under an erupting fissure with, at the very most, one death. **That is the fact. It does not need decorating.**

Today **4,518 people** live out there — **1 January 2026** — and the ferry from **Landeyjahöfn**, open since the summer of **2010**, takes **just over thirty minutes**, against **three hours** by the old route.
say: the Westman Islands out to sea; only Heimaey is inhabited
"Home Island", the one with the town, the volcano and the harbour
"Fire Mountain", the volcano that did not exist before 23 January 1973
the older cone beside it, the one Eldfell grew to match
"Fire Worlds", the museum built over the dug-out houses
the mainland ferry harbour, open since 2010, half an hour out
the dredger that turned a fire hose into an artillery barrage of seawater

cuePerTour.6.0: Look right at 2 o'clock — the Westman Islands out to sea.

block.title: 🛡️ Markarfljót & Hlíðarendi
block.cue: Look left at 10 o'clock — Hlíðarendi above Markarfljót.
block.hook: Those green slopes aren't just a nice view. In the sagas, they were **worth dying for.**
block.point: To your guests it's a farm in the distance. To Icelanders it's a **moral crossroads** still standing in the landscape almost a thousand years later.
block.mic: Out there: grass and sheep. In the sagas: a man who chose his view over his life — and a wife who remembered exactly how she'd been wronged.
block.weather: Weather pivot: "If the hillside has gone, remember that Gunnar turned back for the view. He would not have on a day like this."
bullets: The **Markarfljót** in front of you rises under **Torfajökull**, up in the highlands — not off the two ice caps everyone assumes. *Heima er bezt* puts it at about **75 km** from source to sea. Then again, ask how long it is and you have picked a fight: it is a **braided** river, and Iceland's national map data carries **190 separate channels** all called Markarfljót, adding up to well over 200 km of water. It does not have a course. It has a committee.
What **Eyjafjallajökull** and **Mýrdalsjökull** do is feed it lower down — two ice caps sitting on live volcanoes — which is why it occasionally stops being a river and becomes a **jökulhlaup**.

**2010, and the bit everybody gets wrong.** You will hear that engineers deliberately cut the Ring Road embankment to save the bridge. What *Morgunblaðið* reported at the time is better: **the swollen river broke its own gap** in the flood dyke east of Markarfljót, and that is what took the load off the bridge. The deliberate version is a real Icelandic technique — at **Skeiðará in 1996** they cut **five gaps** in the embankment and planned to cut the road itself in two places — but here, the river did its own engineering and the engineers let it.

Tucked into the far slopes is **Hlíðarendi**, home of **Gunnar**, the finest fighter in **Njáls saga** — the saga claims he could leap his own height in full armour, backwards as well as forwards, which is the kind of thing sagas claim.

Sentenced to exile, Gunnar rode out, glanced back and said the line every Icelander knows: ***"Fögur er hlíðin"*** — fair is the hillside — and I will not go away. That one look cost him everything. He turned back, stayed, and was killed defending his farm.

And the ending is worse than that. Besieged, his bowstring cut, he asked his wife **Hallgerður** for two locks of her hair to twist a new one. She refused — payback for a slap years before — and let him die. A thousand years on, it is still the most quoted argument in Icelandic literature.
say: the braided glacial river below, rising under Torfajökull
the highland ice cap it actually comes from
Gunnar's farm on the far slopes, the hillside he refused to leave
the hero of Hlíðarendi, the finest fighter in the sagas
his wife, who refused him her hair for a new bowstring
"fair is the hillside", the line that killed him
the glacial flood this river turns into

block.title: 🌊 Landeyjar Plains
block.cue: Look right at 2 o'clock — Landeyjar sandur, the plain running away to the sea.
block.hook: We've barely left town and we've already **driven off the map** — this flat land used to be the **bottom of the Atlantic Ocean**.
block.point: Living here means accepting your backyard is the **natural drain for big angry glaciers** — every farm, fence and bridge gets built with **jökulhlaups** in the back of people's minds.
block.mic: "There's nothing here," they say. Under you: old seabed. Ahead: glacial wash-plain. Inland: a ghost coastline. Out there: a saga murder scene. That's a lot of nothing.
block.weather: Weather pivot: "Flat, wet and grey is this plain's default setting. It is a floodplain. It looks like this most of the year."
bullets: It looks like "just flat fields", but you are crossing a giant **flood-deposit fan**, built grain by grain by glacial rivers charging out of the highlands — chiefly the **Markarfljót**.

The name gives it away. **Landeyjar means "land islands"** — the grassy patches that stood up out of the marsh and sand back when the water still owned everything around them. Waves once rolled over where this road runs, and the sea came right up to that **cliff line** inland. Then the land rose, the rivers kept dumping sand, and the coastline **marched south, kilometre by kilometre**.
So the cliffs you can see used to be beach, and the beach is now several kilometres further out. Iceland does not have a coastline so much as a rolling negotiation.

This "empty" plain is also **Njáls saga's stage**. **Bergþórshvoll** — where Njáll and his family were burned alive, around **1011** in the saga's own reckoning — sits out here among the hayfields. Flat, quiet, and a thousand years ago the address of Iceland's most famous house fire. People have dug for it, more than once, and found a burnt layer.
say: "land islands", the flat plain of old seabed we're crossing
the farm out here where Njáll's family was burned alive
the glacial river that built this plain out of the highlands
the glacial flood every fence and bridge out here is built against

cuePerTour.6.0: Look right at 2 o'clock — Landeyjar sandur, the plain running away to the sea.

block.title: 🌋 Eyjafjallajökull
block.cue: Look left at 10–11 o'clock — Eyjafjallajökull and Þorvaldseyri farm.
block.hook: In **2010**, this innocent-looking glacier volcano shut down **air travel for millions** who couldn't even say its name.
block.point: Up there: a peaceful glacier above a postcard farm. In memory: the mountain that turned Europe's airports into campgrounds.
block.mic: A farmer here was digging ash out of his drinking water while airline chief executives were melting down 2,000 km away.
block.weather: Weather pivot: "Cannot see it? Neither could the pilots in 2010, and that was rather the problem."
bullets: It does not look like much: a tidy white lid over green fields. **Veðurstofa Íslands** describes what is actually under there — a cone **about 1,666 metres** high, the volcano itself **25 km long and 15 km wide**, mostly buried in ice, with a **crater about 2.5 km across**. It has been a fairly active volcano for the last **8,000 years**, and its magma runs **all the way from basalt to rhyolite** — which is exactly why it can produce fine, glassy ash instead of tidy lava.

By volcanic standards **2010 was small**: a **VEI 4**, only about **0.27 km³** of ash. But it fired a **plume 8–9 km high** straight into the **jet stream**, and those glassy particles turn jet engines into **expensive sandblasters**. A small volcano in exactly the wrong place, pointing at exactly the wrong wind.

The result was the **worst aviation shutdown in Europe since the Second World War** — **104,000 flights cancelled over eight days, 15 to 22 April**, about **48% of expected European traffic**, roughly **10 million passengers** who simply could not fly, and the airspace of some **20 countries** closed. Europe discovered that volcanoes do not read timetables.

The first hit, though, was local. As meltwater poured off the ice, **500 to 800 people were evacuated overnight** from the farms below, and the ash fell thick enough to turn day into night. At **Þorvaldseyri**, right at the foot, they **milked the cows in respirator masks** and scraped ash off the roofs — and then built a visitor centre, because if a volcano is going to rewrite your year you may as well sell the story back.

And the question every single group asks: **did it set off Katla next door?** Here is the honest answer. The two sit **25 km apart**. Eyjafjallajökull erupted in **1821–1823**, in **1612–1613** and **probably in 920**, and you will very often hear that Katla followed each time — but **Veðurstofa's own page lists those eruptions and does not make that claim**. What is certain is that in **2010 Katla stayed shut**. Treat this mountain as a warning light, not a trigger.
say: the glacier volcano whose 2010 ash cloud grounded European air travel
the farm right at its foot, evacuated overnight in 2010
the far bigger volcano 25 km east of it, which did not follow in 2010
a volcanic cone, which is what Veðurstofa calls this one

block.title: 🪨 Drangurinn
block.cue: Look left at 10 o'clock — Drangurinn, under the cliffs of Eyjafjöll.
block.hook: A rock that **forgot to leave** when the rest of the mountain eroded away — and became a barn, a film set, and an elf hotel.
block.point: A single stone that lets you flip between two ways of seeing Iceland — geology and saga — at the same time.
block.mic: Geologists see a volcanic leftover. Storytellers see a giant's throw. The farmers just saw a free barn with elf staff.
block.weather: Weather pivot: "The rock sits right by the road, so this is one you get whatever the sky is doing."
bullets: **Drangurinn** stands alone in the field like a stubborn leftover: a block of **móberg**, palagonite tuff, the same subglacial-eruption rock that built **Pétursey** further along this coast, left standing when the softer cliff around it weathered away. It is about **300 metres from the farmhouse**, in the home field of **Drangshlíð**, under the **Eyjafjöll** cliffs — which is why it looks dropped there rather than grown there.

The saga version is more fun. **Grettir the Strong**, Iceland's great troublemaking outlaw, is said to have torn it out of the cliff above and thrown it down here, leaving a notch in the ridge behind. Once you have heard that, the notch stops looking like erosion and starts looking like a **missing tooth**.

Locals did not waste a rock this size. They **built turf barns and cowsheds straight up against it**, and the folklore — **Jón Árnason's** collection — says **elves live inside**, that they quietly mind the farmers' cows, and that at calving time they will even **milk them**. The most useful neighbours in Iceland, if you believe it, and rent-free stabling if you do not.

Here is the part that should make the coach laugh: **people have been stopping for this rock for a century.** *Lesbók Morgunblaðsins*, in **1928**, wrote that few things catch a passing traveller's eye like the Drangur at Drangshlíð. Ninety-odd years of buses slowing down for the same stone, and it has not moved an inch.
It later turned up as a location in the Viking film ***Hrafninn flýgur*** — "When the Raven Flies". Even the movies knew a dramatic rock when they saw one.
say: the lone standing rock in the field, with turf barns built against it
the palagonite tuff it is made of, the same rock as Pétursey
Grettir the Strong, the outlaw said to have thrown it here
"When the Raven Flies", the film shot here

block.title: 🧊 Sólheimajökull
block.cue: At Sólheimajökull glacier.
block.hook: This is where the glacier stops being "a nice view from the bus" and turns into a **giant, melting history book.**
block.point: Not a lecture about climate. A tape measure, ninety-four years of readings, and a walk that gets longer every summer.
block.mic: You do not have to take my word for any of this. Somebody wrote it down every year since 1930.
block.weather: Weather pivot: "The ice does not mind the weather. The measuring tape has been out in worse than this since 1930."
bullets: A gravel path pulls you toward **Sólheimajökull**, an outlet tongue of **Mýrdalsjökull** — Iceland's **fourth-largest ice cap**, and the lid on **Katla**. You are standing on the drainpipe of a buried volcano.

Up close the ice isn't white. It's streaked with **black ash bands** from **Katla** and **Eyjafjallajökull**, like a sooty paintbrush dragged across it. Each dark line is a bad year for somebody's washing.

In front sits a **blue-green lagoon** with small icebergs in it. The colour is **glacial flour** — rock ground so fine the water turns to liquid stone-dust. That lagoon is **new**. It is here because the ice is not.

Here is the part nobody makes up, because it is measured. **Somebody has walked out to this ice with a tape measure every year since 1930**, and the numbers are public. Over that whole record the front has pulled back **just under two kilometres — 1,995 metres.** Over the last ten years it has averaged **about 50 metres a year**; the most recent measured year, **2023 to 2024, was 43 metres.** The worst single year on record is **134 metres**, and it has happened **twice** — in **2007–08** and again in **2017–18**.

And here is the bit that gets left out. **It is not a straight line down.** Between **1969 and 1995 this glacier ADVANCED in 23 years out of 29**, putting on **440 metres** — a quarter of a century of growing, in the middle of the record. That is why the measurements matter more than the slogan: real data has a reversal in it, and it still ends where this one ends.
Signs along the path mark where the front used to reach — "here… and here… and here." You have just walked **decades of retreat in a few minutes**, and the walk keeps getting longer.
say: the glacier tongue in front of us, pulling back about 50 m a year
Iceland's fourth-largest ice cap, the one this tongue flows from
the volcano buried under that ice cap
the other volcano whose ash streaks this ice black
"snout measurements", the annual survey that produced every number above

block.title: ✈️ The DC-3 Wreck
block.cue: Look right at 2 o'clock — far out on the sand plains.
block.hook: Somewhere out there in the black void is a silver ghost that **Justin Bieber made world-famous** — and that half the internet gets the name of wrong.
block.point: It's a **modern layer on the geology**: Katla built the sandur, the US Navy accidentally parked a plane on it, and social media did the rest.
block.mic: From the bus you mostly see empty blackness. The real story is a crew that iced up over a glacier, glided to the coast, and **lived** — on a plane everyone insists on calling by the wrong name.
block.weather: Weather pivot: "You would not see the wreck from the road on the clearest day of the year. That is what the photograph is for."
bullets: Everyone calls it a "DC-3". It isn't. It is a **US Navy Super DC-3 — a Douglas R4D-8 / C-117D** — same family, the cousin who went to the gym. It has worn the wrong name for fifty years and has long since stopped correcting anybody.

On **21 November 1973** it was flying **Höfn to Keflavík** when **ice choked both carburettors** over the **Vatnajökull** ice cap and both engines quit. The tourist version — that it "ran out of fuel" — is wrong. It iced up, and became, in the crew's own description, a massively overweight glider.

The pilot turned **south for the coast** and put it down on the black sand. **All seven crew walked away.** The Navy stripped out the useful parts and left the bare hull sitting there, which is how you end up with an aeroplane as a landmark.

For decades it was a quiet local curiosity. Then came a **Bieber video in 2015**, the Bollywood hit *Dilwale*, and Instagram, and that was that. **Cars were banned in 2016**, so now you walk a **4 km track each way** across old ocean floor in order to touch a plane with no wings.

⚠️ And that walk deserves respect. **Eight kilometres round trip across open sandur with no shelter of any kind** — not a tree, not a rock, not a wall — and no vehicle coming to get you. The weather out there can change while you are still walking out. It is a proper expedition dressed up as a photo stop.

🎬 **On screen:** a music-video magnet — **Justin Bieber's** "I'll Show You" (2015), Sigur Rós's *Heima* documentary (2007), and Bollywood's *Dilwale* ("Gerua") all used the plane and the black desert around it.
say: the black outwash plain the wreck sits on, built by Katla
the ice cap it was crossing when the engines iced up
an outwash plain of glacial sand; the word English borrowed for it

block.title: ⛰️ Pétursey
block.sub: The Island That Got Left Behind
block.cue: Look right at 1–2 o'clock — the steep, isolated mountain.
block.hook: A **288-metre lump of frozen explosion** that used to be a real island — submarine volcano, sailors' landmark, and a cave with a chapel, a shieling and a monster in it. **Most mountains never have a CV that long.**
block.point: Geology, a lost coastline, a cave chapel and a monster — all stacked on one piece of frozen ash.
block.mic: Most mountains have a Wikipedia stub. **Pétursey has a CV.**
block.weather: Weather pivot: "If the mountain is in cloud you are seeing exactly what it was for. It was a sea mark, and sailors mostly needed it in bad visibility."
bullets: **Pétursey** is **móberg** — the ash-and-rubble palagonite rock you get when a volcano **erupts under water or ice**. Hot magma met cold sea, shattered mid-blast, and cemented into these steep walls. Same recipe as nearby **Drangurinn**. **Landmælingar Íslands** puts the summit crags at **288 metres**.

It was not always a mountain in a field. **Its old name was Háey — "the high island"** — and Iceland's national place-name record says so outright: *Pétursey var nefnd Háey eða Eyjan há í gömlum ritum.* The Atlantic really did go all the way round it, and sailors steered by it, until **Katla's black sand filled the gap and stranded it inland.** The island is still here. The sea moved out.

At the foot on the north side is **Eyjarhellir**, a cave big enough to echo, and the official place-name record for it reads like a short story. There are **ancient man-made marks** inside. Its side chamber is called **Stúkan** — the chapel stall — and was held to be **an old chapel**, until a landslide closed the door on it. **Loðmundur**, the settler at Sólheimar, is said to have kept his **shieling** in there. And the record ends by wondering whether **papar** — Irish monks, here before the Norse — lived in it, and whether the marks in Stúkan are theirs.

It also had a tenant nobody wanted. An **óvættur**, a malevolent thing, lived in Eyjarhellir and was seen before **blizzards and fatal accidents**. It was last seen around **1900**, in the shape of a dog that **grew until it was a troll reaching halfway up the mountain.** Horses refused to pass the cave mouth. A second-sighted farmer named **Indriði** reckoned the creature spent its time fighting the **water-demon of Klifandi** — and that this was the only reason Klifandi had not washed Pétursey's fields away. Which it has, partly, anyway. Even the monster was only doing an adequate job.

The name travelled. A line-fishing boat called **Pétursey** was lost in **March 1941** on passage to Scotland, and was reported sunk. This coast names its boats after its landmarks, and the war took some of them back.
The cliffs still work as a **seabird colony** — fulmars and **puffins** wheeling round it as though it never stopped being an island. Two farms sit at the base: **Eystri-** and **Vestri-Pétursey.**
say: "Peter's Island", the steep 288 m mountain, once a real island
"the high island", its old name, and still the name of its summit crags
the ash-and-rubble palagonite rock it is made of
the cave at its foot, with the chapel, the shieling and the monster
the side chamber in it that was held to be an old chapel
the volcano whose black sand stranded it inland

block.title: ⛪ Skeiðflatarkirkja
block.cue: Look left — small red-roofed church in the fields.
block.hook: This tiny country church is the **DNA** of some of Iceland's most famous modern buildings.
block.point: The story of Reykjavík's iconic architecture doesn't start in the city. It starts on **farms like this**, under the shadow of volcanoes.
block.mic: If you squint, you can almost see Hallgrímskirkja **hiding inside** this little red-roofed church — it just needed a son with a big imagination and a state architect's salary.
block.weather: Weather pivot: "Small red roof, big grey sky. It is the roof you are looking for, not the church."
bullets: This modest church was built by the master carpenter **Samúel Jónsson** — by all accounts a prolific and well-respected house-builder — one of those simple, sturdy rural churches put up to shrug off wind, rain and ash.

His son, **Guðjón Samúelsson**, was born **16 April 1887** and became **húsameistari ríkisins**, the state architect, **from 1915 until he died on 25 April 1950**. Thirty-five years designing the country. The University of Iceland made him an **honorary doctor of philosophy in June 1940**, which is not a thing that usually happens to carpenters' sons from Mýrdalur.

His **Hallgrímskirkja** — the basalt-column church on the Reykjavík hill — took **forty-one years to build** and was **consecrated in 1986**. Guðjón had been dead for **thirty-six** of those years. He drew the most recognisable building in Iceland and never saw it standing.

Look at this roof, then picture that one. You can feel these small rural churches — built plain, built to last, built for weather — echoing in the capital's skyline. Iceland's grandest church is a farm chapel that went to architecture school.
say: the small red-roofed country church in the fields
the master carpenter father who built it
"the state's master builder", the post he held
the basalt-column church on the Reykjavík hill that he designed

block.title: 🚪 Dýrhólaey
block.cue: Look right at 2 o'clock — the high headland with the lighthouse.
block.hook: Ahead on the right is the **front door of the South Coast** — a headland with a hole so big a pilot once flew a plane **clean through it. Three times, because once is an accident.**
block.point: A teaching stop par excellence: glacial plains, old islands and active coastal erosion all visible in **one slow spin of your head.**
block.mic: Dýrhólaey is the hinge where the **volcanoes, the sandur and the ocean** all shake hands — and argue about who built this coastline.
block.weather: Weather pivot: "If the headland has gone you may still catch the light blinking, which is the entire reason it is up there."
bullets: **Dýrhólaey** means "door-hill island", and Iceland's own conservation service describes it precisely: a **120-metre móbergsstapi** — a tuff tuya — **formed in an eruption in the sea**, taking its name from the **arch rock** that from either side looks like an enormous doorway cut in a sheer cliff. Half of it is tuff, **Háey**; half is basalt, **Lágey**. And despite the *-ey*, the "island" on the end of its name, **it is firmly attached to the mainland.** It has been misnamed for a thousand years and nobody has bothered to fix it.
Sailors were less romantic. They called the hole **Portlandið** — or just **Húllið**, the hull.

On top sits a castle-like lighthouse, one of the most powerful lights on this coast, **built in 1927**. It is there because this headland is the first thing a ship coming out of the Atlantic sees, and the last thing it wants to hit.

From up there you can read the whole **Katla Corridor** in one turn of the head — the sandur behind, the **Reynisdrangar** needles ahead, and the Atlantic hurling itself at the basalt. It is a **seabird city**: Dýrhólaey has been a **friðland — a protected nature reserve — since 1978**, all **1.51 km²** of it, and the official reason is not the view, it is the **birds**. Parts close in the nesting season for the puffins, there is a **ranger here all year**, and the rules are the birds' rules.

It was long called the **southernmost point of the mainland** — until **Katla's 1918 flood built Kötlutangi**, which took the title off it for several decades, before the sea carried that sand west again. The volcano moved the goalposts; the Atlantic moved them back.

And in **October 1993**, pilot **Arngrímur Jóhannsson** and MP **Árni Johnsen** flew a light aircraft through the arch. *Morgunblaðið* ran it as "the first aeroplane through Dyrhólaey". Three passes — because if you only do it once, people will say you meant to miss.
🎬 **On screen:** *Game of Thrones* used the beach below as **Eastwatch-by-the-Sea** (Season 7), and it has turned up in *Vikings* and *Beowulf & Grendel* as well.
say: "door-hill island", the 120 m headland with the lighthouse and the arch
its tuff half and its basalt half
the sea-stack needles you can see ahead from the top
the spit Katla's 1918 flood built, the mainland's southernmost point for several decades afterwards
a protected nature reserve; this one dates from 1978

block.title: 🌊 Reynisfjara & Reynisdrangar
block.cue: At the black sand beach.
block.hook: Black sand. A basalt pipe-organ. Sea stacks offshore. **Iceland's most beautiful beach — and its most dangerous. Never turn your back on these waves.**
block.point: One stop: black sand, columnar basalt, wave erosion, and a couple of trolls who lost track of the time — and a sea that has killed people. Awe first, feet planted well back.
block.mic: The trolls froze in the sunrise. The ocean still hasn't lost an argument.
block.weather: Weather pivot: "Bad weather makes this beach more dangerous, not more atmospheric. Stay well back from the water today."
bullets: ⚠️ **Before anything else.** The Icelandic word is **laumualda** — a "sneaking wave". It runs far higher up the beach than the sea in front of you suggests, the water is freezing, and the undertow pulls. **At least five people have been killed by this surf since 2007**, the most recent of them reported in June 2022; a **warning-light system** went up that same summer. Stay high on the dry sand, keep off the wet, and do not turn your back on the water for a photograph. The beach takes about **half a million visitors a year** and has no opinion about any of them.
Under your feet: fine **black volcanic sand** — basalt that met the sea, shattered, and got ground down to grains. **No shells, no coral, just pulverised volcano.**

To one side, **Hálsanefshellir** — the shallow cave with its pipe-organ wall of **hexagonal columns** under the **Garðar** cliff. That is **stuðlaberg**: lava that cooled so slowly it contracted and cracked into near-perfect six-sided pillars. Same trick as the Giant's Causeway, better acoustics.

Out in the surf stand the **Reynisdrangar** sea stacks, the last hard bones of an old headland the sea otherwise chewed away — the "stack" at the end of the crack-cave-arch-stack sequence, and you can see every stage of it from where you stand.

In the legend they are **two night-trolls and a ship**, caught by the sunrise mid-theft and turned to stone. Icelandic trolls are strictly nocturnal; daylight is their kryptonite. They have been standing there mid-heist for a few thousand years, which is the longest anyone has ever been caught in the act.
Above, the **Reynisfjall** cliffs fill with nesting seabirds in summer — **puffins, fulmars and guillemots**. Bring the zoom as well as the wide angle.

🎬 **On screen:** Hollywood's favourite black beach — *Rogue One: A Star Wars Story* (2016), *Star Trek Into Darkness* (2013, standing in for an alien planet), *Noah* (2014), and *Game of Thrones* as the Eastwatch coast, plus several Indian films (*Aadhavan*, *Naayak*).
say: the black sand beach we're on: Iceland's most beautiful and most dangerous
the sea stacks out in the surf; in the legend, two trolls and a ship
the cliff above, full of nesting seabirds in summer
the shallow cave with the pipe-organ wall of hexagonal columns
columnar basalt, the six-sided pillars themselves
the basalt cliff the cave sits under
a sneaker wave, literally a "sneaking wave"; the thing that has killed people here

cuePerTour.7.0: Step off at Reynisfjara — and before anything else: stay high on the sand, well back from the water.

block.title: 🌋 Katla
block.sub: The Sleeping Giant Under the Ice
block.cue: Look left at 9–10 o'clock — Mýrdalsjökull, the ice cap covering Katla.
block.hook: The biggest threat on the South Coast doesn't look like a threat — it's a **white ice cap, peaceful and silent.**
block.point: The most dangerous volcano on the south coast doesn't look like a volcano. It looks like a glacier.
block.mic: Iceland's most polite warning: **the loudest thing she does is wait.**
block.weather: Weather pivot: "Cannot see the ice cap? Neither can the people living under it. That is the whole problem with Katla."
bullets: Under that ice sits **Katla**, and she is not a tidy cone. **Veðurstofa Íslands** puts the system at **about 80 km long**, reaching **around 1,500 m**, with an **ice-filled caldera** and fissure swarms running **northeast towards Síðujökull**. The caldera is not the neat ten-kilometre circle you will read online — that came from a proposed shape in a 1973 paper. The Icelandic geoscience journal **Jökull** describes something elongated, roughly **100 km²**. Either way: the mountain you cannot see is bigger than the mountains you can.

The lid is **Mýrdalsjökull**, Iceland's **fourth-largest ice cap** — **520 km² when it was surveyed in 2019** — sitting on the furnace like several hundred metres of insulation. Being subglacial is the entire danger. She doesn't just throw ash; she **flash-melts a glacier into a flood.** Veðurstofa is blunt about it: without the ice on top, these would probably just be lava eruptions.

She is the **fourth most active volcanic system in Iceland**, with **at least 21 eruptions in the last 1,100 years**. The last one to break through the ice was **1918**. From the settlement to 1918 the **average gap between eruptions was about 50 years**; Jökull's commonly cited range is **every 40 to 80**. It is now **108 years**. Do that sum on a bus and watch the faces change.

An eruption under ice makes a **jökulhlaup**, and the estimates for Katla's peak discharge run to around **300,000 cubic metres a second** — an estimate, not a gauged reading, because nobody has ever stood downstream with a flow meter and lived to publish. Historically those floods came down **Mýrdalssandur**; in prehistory they also came down **Markarfljót**. The town of **Vík** has drilled for this for decades.

**12 October 1918** is the date that rearranged the map. The flood carried so much sediment to the sea that it **pushed the shore south of Hjörleifshöfði out by more than 3 km** — a saga headland that once stood by open water is now stranded **inland**. A volcano that does land reclamation.

Even asleep she exhales. A **2018 study in Geophysical Research Letters** — Ilyinskaya and colleagues, flying instruments over the ice in **2016 and 2017** — measured **12 to 24 kilotonnes of CO₂ a day** coming off Katla, which would make her one of the largest measured carbon sources among the world's *non-erupting* volcanoes, perhaps **4% of the global total**. Nobody has repeated the measurement since, so treat it as a photograph of two summers, not a live feed.

And the family has a bigger member. The **Eldgjá** eruption, on the same system's fissure swarm, **began around 939 CE** and produced **about 20 km³ of lava and tephra** — Veðurstofa's own figure. For scale, the **Holuhraun eruption of 2014–15**, which most of us watched on the news, made about **1.5 km³**. Eldgjá was over thirteen times that.

🎬 **On screen:** the ice up here doubled as the land **beyond the Wall** in *Game of Thrones* Season 2 — the Night's Watch and Fist of the First Men scenes. They needed somewhere that looked like the end of the world and did not have to build a thing.
say: the volcano under that ice, an 80 km system with an ice-filled caldera
the ice cap covering her, Iceland's fourth-largest, 520 km² in 2019
the glacial outburst flood an eruption under ice makes
"fire gorge", her system's monster, about 20 km³ around 939
the town that has drilled for that flood for decades
